entries.title: White Sox still want the division title, but earning a playoff berth 'would be everything'
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> have grander ambitions than the third wild card spot, or even the American League Central title.</p><p>“If we get to do what we want to do, we’re going to be playing in the ALDS, CS and hopefully the World Series,” said Grant Taylor.</p><p>But assistant general manager Jin Wong was the White Sox executive accompanying the team for their road series in Kansas City on Tuesday. After a victory and a Rangers loss to the Mets lowered the White Sox' magic number for clinching a wild card berth to two entering Wednesday, Chris Getz and Josh Barfield flew into town to join him.</p><p>It doesn’t appear Getz is in town to deliver a postgame message to the team about the importance of staying focused on catching the Cleveland Guardians. The franchise’s first playoff appearance in five years is something to celebrate.</p><p>“It would be everything,” starter Davis Martin said of the Sox clinching a playoff spot. “We've been wrapped up in the division [race], and that's still something that's been our goal since the beginning. But from a standpoint of where we've been the last three years, just to be a part of something like that and to turn around and be the spark plug to something that maybe continues on for five, six, seven, eight years, it's just exciting.”</p><p>Martin is the longest-tenured player on the White Sox, which only means he’s been around since 2022, but plenty of suffering has been packed into that window of time. He can remember being asked “how do you sleep at night” in interviews in 2024, as if playing for a bad baseball team was a black mark on his life. Even friends and family asked if he’d rather just be traded, just to get away.</p><p>“I told all of them: my goal would be to be a part of the team that turns it around,” Martin told the Sun-Times. “To be in the situation we are now, which felt like a pipe dream two years ago, and now it’s sitting there looking at you in the face. It's incredible.”</p><p>There’s historical precedent for how incredible it is for the White Sox to make the playoffs at all. No team in MLB history has reached the postseason after three-consecutive 100-loss seasons, and the expanded playoff field can only do so much to blunt that accomplishment. But Sox players — when they’re not quoting their dire preseason projections — more sharply note the difference in how it <i>feels</i> to be part of this team, compared to just two years prior.</p><p>“In the beginning of the year, nobody really believed in us and what we are doing and now look at us,” said All-Star third baseman Miguel Vargas. “If we do it, it’s going to mean a lot for us. I think it’s a special moment.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable has been cherishing moments in places like Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City and Busch Stadium in St. Louis that lack prominent out-of-town scoreboards to distract his players, and himself. But on nights like Wednesday, where the result of Rangers-Mets could dictate whether it’s possible for the Sox to clinch a historic playoff berth, and the result of Guardians-Red Sox could mean there’s a chance to pull ahead in the AL Central, it’s hard not to get curious.</p><p>"It's been a challenge the last couple of weeks, honestly,” Venable said. “It's part of this. It's the position that we've earned, that we're in.”</p><p>It will also say a lot about what the Sox are doing in the visitor’s locker room after the game. Teams like the Dodgers or Yankees might celebrate a Wild Card spot with a polite champagne toast and a short speech about larger goals. A team like the White Sox, with their shared history, will go a different route.</p><p>“It’s not really our speed,” Martin said of a polite toast. “We kind of do everything full-go. I don’t expect it to be casual.”</p>

entries.title: Idaho authorities present new lead on Tylenol murders tied to recently identified man
entries.summary: <p>A recently identified Idaho man who died in 1982 — known as the “Unknown Wanderer” — could have ties to the four-decade-old Tylenol murders case, according to law enforcement agencies in Idaho.</p><p>Dr. Matthew Francis Betkouski died of cyanide poisoning in the pews of a Boise church in 1982, with $1,900 cash and recently dyed hair, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://adacounty.id.gov/sheriff/news/acso-solves-decades-old-unknown-wanderer-cold-case/" target="_blank" >Ada County sheriff’s office</a>.</p><p>The agency, which had been searching for the man's identity for decades, is being careful not to officially name Betkouski as a suspect in the murders even though Sheriff Matt Clifford announced evidence is going to be presented as part of an upcoming Roku documentary titled “Unmasking the Tylenol Killer” set to premiere Oct. 9.</p><p>The Ada County sheriff’s office is also sharing relevant evidence with Chicago police that may be connected to the murders.</p><p>“More information does exist in this case that we won’t be releasing today,” said Tim Cooper, a detective with the Ada County sheriff's office. “Our goal today is to generate leads in this case or others.”</p><p>Seven Chicago-area people died in September 1982 after ingesting cyanide-laced Tylenol. Johnson & Johnson recalled every form of the over-the-counter drug and created more tamper-proof pills and packaging as law enforcement searched for the culprit.</p><p>Chicago police Wednesday confirmed it had been in contact with the Ada County authorities regarding the case to “determine whether there is a connection to the Tylenol murders investigation, which remains an open cold case.”</p><p>James Lewis, a longtime leading suspect, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for extortion nearly a year later for demanding $1 million from Johnson & Johnson “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2023/7/10/23789606/james-lewis-prime-suspect-in-tylenol-tampering-cases-dead-at-76" target="_blank" ><u>to stop the killings</u></a>" and maintained his innocence until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/10/23790603/tylenol-james-lewis-extortion-cyanide-mcnamee-chicago-obituary" target="_blank" >he died in 2023</a>.</p><div Lewis, the suspect in the 1982 Tylenol poisonings that killed seven people in the Chicago area and triggered a nationwide scare died in 2023. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>(Keith Myers/The Kansas City Star, distributed by the Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>No one has been charged in the case. </p><p>But the latest information could reveal new potential leads in the case.</p><p>Idaho investigators traced evidence — and eventually a DNA match — to Betkouski's brother after police positively identified the “Unknown Wanderer."</p><p>Betkouski struggled with mental illness throughout his life, though a traumatic brain injury in 1974 worsened his condition, investigators said. He wrote about his struggles with schizophrenia and depression, and that he was convinced a euphoria he gained from imagining scenes of violence could cure him.</p><p>Photos show him in Chicago in December 1981, though investigators couldn't place him in the city during the time of the murders.</p><p>In 1975, Betkouski, a chemist, moved to Jacksonville, Florida, for work, where he was reported by colleagues to management for talking about committing the “perfect crime” and suicide via cyanide, investigators said.</p><p>He was fired from Lockheed in 1982 for taking home unauthorized materials from the lab and over an “incident” at a local pharmacy in which he tried to obtain pills for an “experiment,” investigators said. A co-worker at the time reported him for allegedly saying poison could be slipped into pharmaceuticals.</p><p>A search of his childhood bedroom, where he stayed with his brother occasionally as an adult, turned up a map of Chicago made in the 1970s as well as a bottle of sodium cyanide — a different kind than was used in the Chicago area murders, investigators said. </p><p>Idaho investigators later connected with Arlington Heights police regarding their Tylenol murders cases. They also reached out to the Las Cruces Police Department in New Mexico, which also had unsolved cyanide poisoning in pharmaceuticals cases before the Chicago area murders.</p><p>Seven weeks before his death, Betkouski disappeared from his Las Cruces home. He then sold his car near the Mexico border shortly after and was subsequently found dead in the Boise church.</p><p>Chicago police ask that tips about the case be submitted to CPDTip.com or by calling 800-535-7867.</p><p>“This isn’t over, and what you’ve heard today could take months or years to work through,” Clifford said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/10/23790603/tylenol-james-lewis-extortion-cyanide-mcnamee-chicago-obituary" target="_blank" >Tylenol suspect James Lewis said anyone could have poisoned those capsules — then explained how</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2023/7/11/23790874/tylenol-killings-james-lewis-highland-park-chicago-unabomber-mcveigh-domestic-terrorism" target="_blank" >STEINBERG: Tylenol killings and the mystery of murder</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Alex Bregman ‘felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face,’ working to make quick return to Cubs
entries.summary: <p>Trust me, you don’t want to be <b>Alex Bregman</b> right now.</p><p>“I felt like I got hit by a baseball bat to the face, pretty much,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ third baseman said Wednesday, three days after he took a foul ball to the face while standing on deck during a game in Cincinnati.</p><p>Bregman and the Cubs have said they’ve received relative <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/22/cubs-alex-bregman-not-on-injured-list-regular-season-playoffs" >“great news” since</a>, in terms of a potential return, one that could come as soon as this weekend.</p><p>But while that would be a boost to the Cubs’ chances as they approach the most meaningful games of their season, he’s dealing with some significant aftereffects, with multiple facial fractures.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/T7ZbU-xz3UU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Alex Bregman on taking a baseball to the face"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“The pain’s been fine,” Bregman said. “I guess I fractured something right by the nerve in my face, so the whole left side of my face has been a little bit numb. As soon as the swelling goes down, I’m sure I’ll feel the breaks a little bit more.</p><p>“But all in all, I’m super lucky that it hit where it hit. A lot of gratitude, because if it was a few centimeters higher, it could have been detrimental.”</p><p>And here’s some more body horror:</p><p>“There’s a lot of fluid in my face,” Bregman said. “If I move, the fluid moves. If I’m bouncing up and down, my face feels like it’s bouncing up and down.”</p><p>All that is to illustrate what Bregman’s dealing with. But being the lauded hard-worker he is, it’s little surprise that he’s champing at the bit to get back in the lineup.</p><p>“[Tuesday] was brutal. I wanted to play,” he said. “I hope [to play this weekend]. We’ll see. One step at a time. I don’t know. I’m going to try to get in there [Wednesday].”</p><p>That last line was a joke, in case you were wondering. Bregman still has a lot to test out to see how he feels and how realistic such a quick comeback is.</p><p>“He’s doing well. But we’ve got to take some steps here,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “I’m excited how he feels, and he’s excited. But he still needs to feel some things. He hasn’t run around yet, and he’s got to do that. He’s got to know what it feels like.</p><p>“We’ve got to be careful, and we’ve got to go through the proper steps.”</p><h3><b>Bummer of a bunt</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> entered Wednesday with a .176 batting average in his last 18 games.</p><p>He got a chance to help produce a run in extra innings Tuesday, but he popped up a bunt attempt with two men on and nobody out in the 10th inning of an eventual 8-2 loss.</p><p>It’s a relative nit to pick from a game in which the Cubs went 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position, but with a lot on the line in the season’s final week, it could be among the moments that loom large.</p><p>“These are the moments you prepare for,” Shaw said. “I know that I’m going to have a situation again where I’m going to have to put a bunt down. We all know what the stakes are. All we can do is keep preparing for these moments.</p><p>“An experience like this is going to help the next time I’m in that situation, and that’s all you can walk away with.”</p><h3><b>Palencia back?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Since allowing seven runs in his first five outings after a lengthy IL stint, righty reliever <b>Daniel Palencia</b> hasn’t allowed an earned run in seven straight appearances, helpful as the Cubs look for their bullpen to stabilize before the postseason begins.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Struggling at the end of a great year, White Sox reliever Sean Newcomb feels he's gotten too predictable
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The <b>Sean Newcomb </b>fastball that Tigers infielder <b>Hao-Yu Lee</b> hit for a game-tying home run last Friday against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> sizzled in at 96.7 mph.</p><p>That was frustrating, but also answered a question for a reliever who has already logged 88 innings on the year.</p><p>“It’s not a stuff thing,” Newcomb told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Instead, Newcomb attributes a 10.80 ERA in September to becoming too predictable. His four-seam fastball has been one of the best pitches in the sport, but Lee homered on the fifth four-seamer of that at-bat.</p><p>Newcomb has struggled to land his slurve to get ahead in counts too, but feels this stretch resembles an earlier point of the season when he was getting beat on too many fastballs.</p><p>“The frustrating part is me not realizing it right away,” Newcomb said. “Pushing through it instead of taking a step back, looking at the big picture.”</p><h3><b>Opening jitters</b></h3><p>Before tossing two scoreless innings on Wednesday, Newcomb’s only scoreless appearance in September was also the only scoreless outing for a White Sox “opener” in their last four usages, as <b>Bryan Hudson</b> was touched up for four runs (three earned) on Wednesday night before giving way to <b>Erick Fedde</b>.</p><p>The Sox have prioritized handedness matchups in the first inning all season, with Wednesday being their MLB-leading 31st use of an opener, and show no signs of backing down.</p><p>“It's an approach that we feel strongly about, specifically with Fedde,” said manager Will Venable. “Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. But it's something we feel strongly gave us the best chance today.”</p>

entries.title: Kevin Gausman bangs up shoulder, Cubs lose another to Marlins: ‘The baseball gods are going to test you’
entries.summary: <p>If back-to-back losses with a chance to clinch a playoff spot weren’t frustrating enough for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, here’s a new potential complication at the very end of the regular season.</p><p>Kevin Gausman – the righty pitcher who headlined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Jed Hoyer’s trade-deadline haul</a> and figured to be a candidate to log significant playoff innings after helping the Blue Jays to the World Series last season – banged his left shoulder while making a diving play at third base in the sixth inning of Wednesday’s 3-2 loss to the Marlins. He exited the game with the trainer.</p><p>Is it a big deal? Something that could possibly impact his effectiveness or availability come the start of the postseason, just a few days away?</p><p>The best Gausman and the Cubs had Wednesday night after the game was that they’ll wait and see.</p><p>“I dislocated this shoulder in high school, a long time ago. I didn’t necessarily do the exact same thing, but I just kind of banged it good,” Gausman said. “I felt fine until I stood up to check the other runner, and it felt like the left shoulder was pretty weak at that point.</p><p>“It still feels pretty weak, but we’ll see how it feels tomorrow and get some treatment. Hopefully, it’s just a couple-day thing.</p><p>“I hope I wake up and feel great tomorrow. But you never know. I’ll get on some medicine and get some treatment, try to get in front of it tonight. It’s just a wait-and-see type thing.”</p><p>Though they hope it’s nothing serious, the Cubs can’t afford another pitching headache at the moment, not with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-red-sox-friday-doubleheader-boston-weather-forecast-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoffs-postseason" >nasty weather in Boston jumbling up their final series</a> of the regular season against the Red Sox this weekend. Those games – two of which will now be played in a Friday doubleheader – will be meaningful, with the NL wild-card standings bunched up and home-field advantage in the opening-round, best-of-three series up for grabs.</p><p>It’ll be challenging enough for the Cubs to get through the weekend, with its scheduling chaos, and set up their playoff rotation the way they want to. Anything limiting Gausman would make matters that much more complicated.</p><p>But the Cubs have to get to the playoffs first, still not something that seems unlikely; they’d have to lose all of their final four games, with the Diamondbacks winning their last four, to completely collapse and miss the postseason altogether.</p><p>That has been what’s happened in the first two games of the regular season’s final week, though, with the Cubs dropping each of the first two contests in a home series with the sub-.500 Marlins, an opponent that seemingly offered an opportunity to punch their playoff ticket, certainly when compared to this weekend’s foe, the playoff-bound Red Sox.</p><p>But the offense has gone as cold as the Wrigley Field conditions at a bad time, with the Cubs following up Tuesday’s 1-for-18 showing with runners in scoring position by going 1-for-8 in such situations Wednesday, Dansby Swanson’s broken-bat two-run single only briefly getting the Cubs out of trailing position before a video-reviewed double-play ball was flipped into an RBI ground out that gave the Marlins the lead for good in the next inning.</p><p>“It always seems like the baseball gods are going to test you, and it always seems to come at a time when you don’t want it to,” Gausman said. “But those are the things that are going to happen at this time of the year. It’s how you bounce back when those things do happen, when you get punched in the face.</p><p>“This group, since I’ve been here, has been resilient, and they were a lot before I was here. You can bank on those guys being ready to go.”</p>

entries.title: Girl sexually assaulted on way to school in Brainerd
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a teen boy carrying a clear bookbag who sexually assaulted a girl walking to her elementary school in Brainerd on the Far South Side Wednesday morning. </p><p>She was walking to Fort Dearborn Elementary around 7:50 a.m. Wednesday in the 1300 block of West 91st Street when the boy then forced her into an alley and sexually assaulted her, Chicago police said.</p><p>The teen was described as 13 to 14 years old with dreadlocks with orange tips, wearing a black jacket or black long sleeve shirt with white writing, gray pants and carrying a clear school bookbag, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact detectives at 312-492-3810.<br></p>

entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> experts make their picks for the "Monday Night Football" game against the Eagles:</p><h3><b>Patrick Finley</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 21-20:</b> We interrupt the Bears’ quarterback carousel to whisper the following<i>: Are the Eagles good?</i> They beat the Commanders by two in Week 1 and the terrible Titans by four last week. The two are 0-4 and have been outscored by 36 this year. <b>Season</b>: 0-2.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p><b>Eagles, 25-20:</b> Assuming the Bears don’t get Caleb Williams back, they’re hoping Tyson Bagent will clear the concussion protocol in time to start. Otherwise it’s Case Keenum. That’s too much uncertainty against an opponent that’s 52-18 over the last five seasons. <b>Season:</b> 1-1.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>Eagles, 21-17: </b>In a must-win (OK, pivotal) game between two semi-desperate (OK, semi-underachieving) teams, the “drama” intangible is usually the determining factor. And the Bears got more drama (OK, bad luck) than the Eagles right now. <b>Season: </b>1-1.</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>Eagles, 24-16:</b> Caleb Williams isn't going to play, is he? No. N-O. Negatory, Rory. Book it. Etch it in stone. At least, I don't think he'll play. Lord, he really shouldn't. I'm rolling with Jalen Hurts. <b>Season</b>: 1-1.</p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>Eagles, 24-10</b>: Andy Dalton isn’t walking through the Bears’ locker-room door. Neither is Nick Foles, Chase Daniel or Brian Hoyer, all of them former Bears backup QBs who led the way to some unlikely victories. Actually, Dalton COULD walk in — he’s with the Eagles. Come on over! <b>Season: </b>1-1.<br></p>

Trump, once again, retaliates against journalists who offend him
entries.summary: <p>"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117308890736529824" target="_blank" >declared</a> Monday. "It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS."</p><p>Trump was attempting to rebut the criticism provoked by his <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006" target="_blank" >announcement</a> Friday that he was "banning" CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico "from the White House," with "other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." But his defense merely confirmed his long-standing contempt for the freedom he claims to cherish.</p><p>If you don't cover me the way I like, Trump says, I will not let you cover me at all. </p><p>"It's difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment," <a class="Link" href="https://freedom.press/issues/fpf-comments-on-trumps-media-ban-announcement/" target="_blank" >said</a> Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4f0000" name="module-4f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The targeted news outlets responded with a First Amendment <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754/gov.uscourts.dcd.296754.1.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> that was assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee who figured in an earlier legal skirmish between the president and the press. During his first term, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2018/11/16/federal-judge-rules-trump-white-house/" target="_blank" >revoked</a> CNN reporter Jim Acosta's White House press pass, later <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/judge-hands-cnn-victory-in-its-bid-to-restore-jim-acostas-white-house-press-pass/2018/11/16/8bedd08a-e920-11e8-a939-9469f1166f9d_story.html" target="_blank" >explaining</a> that Acosta was not treating him with the "respect" he deserved.</p><p>In response to a CNN <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.201611/gov.uscourts.dcd.201611.1.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a>, Kelly issued a temporary restraining order <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/judge-hands-cnn-victory-in-its-bid-to-restore-jim-acostas-white-house-press-pass/2018/11/16/8bedd08a-e920-11e8-a939-9469f1166f9d_story.html" target="_blank" >blocking</a> Acosta's banishment on <a class="Link" href="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/99/CNN_v._Trump_transcript_2018-11-16.pdf" target="_blank" >due process grounds</a>. The White House avoided a full airing of CNN's First Amendment claims by backing down. After it restored Acosta's press pass, CNN <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/8169022/cable-news-network-inc-v-trump/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> to drop the lawsuit.</p><p>Shortly after beginning his second term, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/12/trump-bans-ap-from-oval-office-for-not-saying-gulf-of-america/" target="_blank" >barred</a> Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and White House briefings because the organization had refused to start calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf America, the name the president <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-names-that-honor-american-greatness/" target="_blank" >prefers</a>. Two months later, another Trump-appointed judge, Trevor N. McFadden, <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.277682/gov.uscourts.dcd.277682.46.0.pdf" target="_blank" >issued</a> a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the AP ban, saying the organization was likely to succeed in its claims that the White House had engaged in unconstitutional retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.</p><p>The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit partially <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cadc.41932/gov.uscourts.cadc.41932.01208746547.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >stayed</a> McFadden's order in June 2025, drawing a distinction between "limited spaces" such as the Oval Office and "events open to all credentialed White House journalists," such as East Room press conferences. The appeals court heard oral argument in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69869862/associated-press-v-taylor-budowich/" target="_blank" >case</a> last November but has not issued a decision yet.</p><p>The bans that Trump announced last week go at least as far as his retaliation against the AP. And it was clear from his remarks that he would like to go even further.</p><p>"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States," Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006" target="_blank" >wrote</a> on Truth Social. "I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day," he <a class="Link" href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-remarks-healthcare-drug-prices-oval-office-september-18-2026/" target="_blank" >told</a> reporters. "There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories."</p><p>That attitude is consistent with Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/18/how-the-fcc-became-the-speech-police/" target="_blank" >oft-repeated threats</a> to revoke broadcast licenses in response to news coverage he views as unfair. Brendan Carr, the Trump-appointed chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/26/brendan-carrs-vendetta-against-abc-conflates-the-public-interest-with-trumps-personal-grievances/" target="_blank" >taken steps</a> toward delivering on those threats, based on the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/22/trumps-threats-to-yank-broadcast-licenses-are-part-of-a-speech-chilling-intimidation-campaign/" target="_blank" >premise</a> that broadcasters are legally obligated to please the president.</p><p>Trump's banishment of disfavored news organizations extends that assault to other media. Unlike broadcasters, cable outlets and newspapers are not subject to the "public interest" obligation that Trump and Carr conflate with a duty to avoid offending the president.</p><p>Trump also has tried to intimidate news organizations with lawsuits preposterously claiming that journalism he does not like qualifies as <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/11/18/court-rejects-trump-big-lie-defamation-lawsuit-00656548" target="_blank" >defamation</a> or <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/04/01/trumps-war-on-the-press/" target="_blank" >consumer fraud</a>. According to Trump, even <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-trump-administrations-1-7-billion-national-guard-deployments-fail-to-reduce-urban-crime/" target="_blank" >questioning</a> the effectiveness of his National Guard deployment in the District of Columbia can <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/31/a-liberal-think-tank-and-an-air-force-major-are-trumps-latest-targets-for-speech-policing/" target="_blank" >expose you</a> to a $5 billion defamation lawsuit.</p><p>Trump said he was "proud to announce" the sanctions against CNN, MS NOW and Politico. He should instead be embarrassed to indulge in such vendettas, which expose not only his thin-skinned pettiness but also his disregard for the First Amendment rights he <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/restoring-freedom-of-speech-and-ending-federal-censorship/" target="_blank" >pretends</a> to defend.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cc0000" name="module-cc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Press will prevail against Trump's attacks
entries.summary: <p>“To offend a strong man, tell him a lie. To offend a weak man, tell him the truth.”</p><p>That quote, often attributed to Marcus Aurelius, one of the great Stoics, perfectly encapsulates the very troubling and sad moment we’re in, and the very troubling and sad president we’re dealing with.</p><p>For all his bluster, Donald Trump is inarguably weak and small. His ego is easily bruised; his feelings are easily hurt. He’s been this way for a long time, and as Americans living in the Trump era, we’ve all come to see how deeply insecure, petty and vengeful he can be.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-260000" name="module-260000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>His late-night social media rants lashing out at enemies both real and imagined; his impetuous and impolitic attacks on longtime allies who don’t roll over for him; his reckless primarying of his own party members who dare break from him, even if momentarily.</p><p>Hell, you could even say his very presidency is the result of an otherwise harmless roast by former President Barack Obama at the 2011 White House Correspondents Dinner that he took too personally.</p><p>But when things are going particularly badly for him, his skin is at its paper thinnest, and it shows.</p><p>Last week, Trump announced on social media that he was banning three news outlets — MS NOW, Politico and CNN, where I work — from covering the White House. He hasn’t said why those particular outlets were targeted, giving the impression that this might not have been all that well thought out. Imagine that.</p><p>It does coincide, however, with Trump’s steadily sinking approval numbers, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-approval-rating-hits-all-time-low-12467727" target="_blank" >just this week</a> hit an abysmal record low, falling below 30% according to one poll.</p><p>Believe it or not, focusing on ballrooms and buildings, invading Greenland and Canada, suing political enemies and chasing crypto deals while we’re in an ill-advised war and most Americans are stretching to afford basic necessities, have not endeared him to voters.</p><p>It’s almost as if ignoring his key promises to voters — to lower inflation, to lower the cost of goods, to never get us into another war — has turned them off.</p><p>So, stuck in a bed of his own making with nowhere to go, he’s lashing out, this time at the press, simply for covering the bad decisions he’s made and their impact on voters.</p><p>But trying to punish or sideline the press will not change the fact that he and Republicans are in deep trouble. All it does is make him look brittle, desperate and weak.</p><p>It’s also a deeply disingenuous effort. Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117308890736529824" target="_blank" >justified</a> his tantrum by saying the press is both “purposeful” and “fully coordinated” in reporting “fiction and lies.”</p><p>There’s a legal mechanism for the thing he’s talking about, and tellingly, he isn’t using it. Because, if true, what he’s describing is the textbook definition of actual malice, the legal bar used for defamation cases.</p><p>But he’s not suing the press, because this isn’t about the law, but rather his feelings. And it’s simply not our job to protect his feelings, or only publish news that makes him feel good. We’re not his parents or his kindergarten teachers.</p><p>He can throw all the fits he wants, and there’s no doubt his continual attacks on the press have had a chilling effect, but I know one thing: Ultimately, the press will win this battle.</p><p>He may wish he were president of Russia or North Korea, where the free press doesn’t exist and state media tells only positive stories about Dear Leader, but here in America, the press is protected. Here, Americans want to live in a democracy, not a dictatorship. And here, we expect our political leaders to be able to take a metaphorical punch. Especially if the “punch” in question is simply the truth.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6d0000" name="module-6d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Feels like I have no choice but to let irresponsible daughter move in
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a widow who lost my husband 15 years ago. When my husband died, we had a daughter and one grandson. My daughter, a single mom, later had another son.</p><p>I have my own business and have worked hard these many years to help support my daughter, who is financially irresponsible. She has been evicted four times in the past 10 years, had two cars repossessed and can't seem to keep a job for even a year. I am at my wits' end. I need to stop helping her financially because it's affecting my financial and mental health. She doesn't have a job and can't get her own place, so I feel I have no choice but to let her move in with me. I want to put a limit on how long she can stay. What should I do? — <i>SUBJUGATED IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR SUBJUGATED:</b> Do not allow your daughter to move in with you. If she does, you will never get rid of her. Give her a certain amount of money for shelter and make it plain that she must use it to find a place to live (if only temporarily). Because it's the last handout she'll receive, she must get a job to support herself and her children. Then let her live the life she has chosen for herself. If you don't, you will be your dysfunctional daughter's prisoner until the day you die.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Throughout my professional career, I was a quality assurance engineer with the task of analysis and corrective actions. If something broke or an error was made (for example, a worker's hand getting caught in a machine), I'd try to identify a fix so it wouldn't happen again. I am now retired and still tend to approach things with the same attitude.</p><p>I often get frustrated when someone makes an error and there's no corrective action, admission that a mistake was made or even a small apology. I recently discovered an error on my financial accounts and asked the bank how this was overlooked even after I had pointed out the error prior to the account being processed. Abby, I was completely ignored and never received any feedback. What's the best way to ask someone for an explanation concerning what actions were taken to ensure the error does not happen again? — <i>KEEN ON QUALITY</i></p><p><b>DEAR KEEN ON QUALITY:</b> In your line of work, safety was the top priority. You developed a zero-tolerance attitude toward errors because it was literally a matter of life and limb. Outside that environment, however, you may find it helpful to remember that the stakes are not nearly so high.</p><p>No permanent harm came of the bank error. You are right that it would be best if the bank reviewed its procedures to avoid future errors, but that's their job, not yours. Having corrected the error in a timely fashion, the bank owes you no further explanation. Trust that, in the future, they will do their best to improve without your help (but always check your statements).</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

Wacker Dr.<br><b>When</b>: through Sep. 27</p><p>Legendary choreographer John Neumeier devised “Liliom” for his home company, the Hamburg Ballet, adapting the same 1909 Hungarian play that inspired the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical “Carousel,” setting it in neither Budapest nor Maine, but a nameless American city during the Great Depression. In this season opener, the Joffrey Ballet here brings “Liliom” to an American company for the first time after previous productions by only Hamburg and the Czech National Ballet. Neumeier enlisted composer Michel Legrand, a versatile musician known foremost for his film scores (“The Umbrellas of Cherbourg,” “Les Demoiselles de Rochefort,” “Yentl”), to write the music for the ballet. Legrand’s unusual instrumentation calls for both an orchestra in the pit and a jazz big band onstage, an arrangement that foregrounds the music more than in many ballets. After the Joffrey’s success with Neumeier’s “The Little Mermaid” a few years ago, “Liliom” looks likely to be another splash. <i>Tickets from $47.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Michigan Ave.<br><b>When</b>: Sep. 24–26</p><p>The Spanish word “matadora” derives from “matar”: to kill. “Matador,” without the terminal a, is familiar even to non-Spanish speakers as the term for a bullfighter, the killer of the bull (if the fight goes according to plan). The dancemaker INSÉKTA adds an -a to the end, a feminine affix, to title their evening-length world premiere about the suppressed feminine rage of an untameable beast. INSÉKTA, known as Camila Rivero Pooley outside of performing life, graduated in 2018 from Columbia College’s dance program. They staged an earlier version of the work at the Dance Center last year, and then were invited to open the center’s 2026-27 season with the five-dancer piece at its full length. The dance sounds bold — the description of the piece carries a content warning for body horror, harm and sensuality. <i>Tickets from $10.</i></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.visceraldance.com/event-details/t-a-k-e-2026-10-22-19-00" target="_blank" ><b><u>TAKE</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where</b>: 3031 N. Rockwell St.<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 9–25</p><p>“Immersive” is the buzzword in all the arts, as groups try to break our Netflix-and-couch habits with increasingly sensory-filled performances that put audiences up close — and sometimes in — the action. In Chicago, the contemporary company Visceral Dance Chicago has been at the vanguard of the phenomenon. In October, the group remounts founder Nick Pupillo’s “Take,” an evening-length immersive work set in a Rockwell Street event space where dancers weave in and out of an audience positioned around the room. The dancing is vigorous, athletic and in your face. The live music, theatrics and invitation to join the dance party at the end will win over even the most committed couch potato. <i>Tickets from $45.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Once</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where</b>: Studio5, 1934 Dempster St., Evanston<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 16–17</p><p>The dance company The Seldoms, now celebrating its 25th year, always approaches its projects thoughtfully, enlisting strong collaborators and underpinning the work with ideas. The world premiere of the full-length version of “All at Once” unifies six dancers and three percussionists to express the concept of showing all perspectives on a visual subject simultaneously, an idea that is central to cubism. Invoking Pablo Picasso’s foundational painting “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon,” which depicts five nude sex workers with sharp-angled figuration, Seldoms founder and choreographer Carrie Hanson brings angularity and torque to the dance. Percussionist Tim Daisy, a return Seldoms collaborator, composed the music with space for improvisation and chance, inserting an element of unpredictability. Another re-upping collaborator, Lara Miller, designed a progression of costumes that increases in volume throughout the work. It may not be ultimately possible for beings bound to three dimensions to fulfill cubism’s goal of all perspectives at once, but Hanson has at least thought through all the angles. <i>Tickets from Ida B. Wells Dr.<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 17</p><p>Dance Theatre of Harlem, one of the first established Black-focused ballet companies, originally premiered its version of Igor Stravinsky’s Firebird in 1982. In their version of the Russian folktale where the title bird catalyzes the triumph of good over evil, DTH moved the action to the Caribbean, allowing for vibrant designs. The company shelved the ballet for about 20 years until reviving it recently, inviting alumni dancers back to re-create the choreography — originally by the mid-20th-century ballet master John Taras — for the current roster. They tour the revival here, where their Chicago stop-off also represents a return, as it’s their first time here since 2016. The program also includes George Balanchine’s “Donizetti Variations” and appropriately for a show with so many coming-back motifs, “Return,” by the company’s artistic director, Robert Garland. Randolph St.<br><b>When</b>: Nov. 14</p><p>The dance style of Compagnie Hervé Koubi lives somewhere between contemporary dance, gymnastics, capoeira, cheer and breaking. Dancers spin on their heads. They are launched through the air by their fellow dancers. They do handsprings and flips. But it’s fundamentally dance under the ample pyrotechnics, one step over the dividing line from circus, waving at Cirque du Soleil on the other side. “Sol Invictus,” the work the company is currently touring, takes its name from the sun god of the ancient Roman empire known as the “unconquered,” and the costumes have a tunic kind of flair that makes sure not to get in the way of flaunting abs and pecs. At earlier stops on the tour, reviewers raved about the part of the performance that involves a huge, shiny gold cloth that the dancers spin on and around, swirling and billowing. <i>Tickets from $40.</i></p><p><i>Cassie Walker Burke contributed reporting. </i></p>

entries.title: What happened at South Chicago Chapel after decomposing bodies were found?
entries.summary: <p>The gruesome discovery of 56 decomposing bodies at South Chicago Chapel in South Deering has raised concerns about the regulation of Illinois funeral homes. How did such neglect happen? And what’s being done about it?</p><h3>What happened at South Chicago Chapel funeral home?</h3><p>In August, Illinois authorities <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" ><u>shut down</u></a> South Chicago Chapel in South Deering after receiving a tip that owners Clark and Johanna Morgan were improperly storing bodies. Inside the funeral home, investigators found dozens of bodies in various stages of decomposition.</p><p>After the investigation, the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer’s license, and the agency is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/21/south-chicago-chapel-johanna-clark-morgan-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-revocation-hearing" ><u>seeking to revoke</u></a> it permanently.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" >The department</a> found the funeral home, 2939 E. 95th St., was “a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare.” It alleged South Chicago Chapel let “multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions, including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies.”</p><h3>Have South Chicago Chapel’s owners been in trouble before?</h3><p>Yes. The August shutdown was the second time in two years authorities have responded to allegations of misconduct against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" ><u>Clark and Johanna Morgan</u></a>.</p><p>In early 2025, the state shut down Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights, also operated by the Morgans, for mishandling the remains of about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" ><u>100 people</u></a>.</p><p>That prompted a new state law expanding the regulatory authority of the Illinois comptroller’s office, which, in a quirk of state responsibilities, oversees crematories in addition to its fiscal duties.</p><p>There were other <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/01/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-clark-johanna-morgan" ><u>red flags</u></a> over the years involving the Morgans:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3c7036d5-b75b-11f1-af38-bfba948b12b7"><li>Evergreen Park police found two bodies in the Morgans’ van on their residential block in 2024.<br></li><li>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Clark Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer license in 2018 due to failure to file or pay state income taxes.<br></li><li>In April 2024, the agency fined Clark Morgan $10,000 and revoked his license due to “unprofessional conduct” and practicing on an expired license. <br></li></ul><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3c705de0-b75b-11f1-af38-bfba948b12b7"><li>South Chicago Chapel had a history of failed building inspections. In addition, city building inspectors hadn’t done an annual inspection for the past four years. <br></li><li>Property tax bills were also delinquent for the past two years, and the Illinois Department of Revenue issued four liens on the Morgans’ home from 2022 to 2026.<br></li></ul><h3>What happened at Bohemian National Cemetery?</h3><p>In a separate case earlier this summer,<b> </b>investigators from the state comptroller’s office visited <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/bohemian-national-cemetery-under-investigation-for-improperly-stored-remains-equipment-failures" ><u>Bohemian National Cemetery</u></a><b> </b>in North Park after a July 21 tip. They found “multiple equipment failures and some human remains waiting to be cremated that were not maintained at the proper temperature,” according to a statement from the comptroller’s office.</p><p>By the end of July, the comptroller’s office had shut down Bohemian. The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation was “made aware” that South Chicago Chapel used the crematorium so “proactively conducted an on-site visit” to the funeral home, the agency said in a statement to the Sun-Times.</p><p>In the wake of recent investigations at Bohemian and Heights Crematory, Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza said she was “thankful” a new state law taking effect Jan. 1 will allow her office to “summarily suspend a crematory license without a prior hearing and immediately inspect the premises and records in egregious cases.”</p><div " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5be5386/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6916x3881+0+365/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F4f%2F99eb1aa94bbb9faa19faf5376da1%2Ffuneralremains-260831-13.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7160c1c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6916x3881+0+365/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F4f%2F99eb1aa94bbb9faa19faf5376da1%2Ffuneralremains-260831-13.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5be5386/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6916x3881+0+365/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F4f%2F99eb1aa94bbb9faa19faf5376da1%2Ffuneralremains-260831-13.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Sisters Franquella (left) and Marshawna Campbell stand with their mother’s urn outside the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office in August. They went there to ask about the location of their mother’s remains. The two believe their mother’s remains are not in the urn, which contains a bag full of what they suspect are rocks, not ashes. The bag is labeled “Bohemian National Cemetery.” The two said they signed with Planet Green Cremations to handle their mother’s remains and do not know how South Chicago Chapel or Bohemian National Cemetery got involved in the process.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Who oversees Illinois’ funeral homes and crematories?</h3><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation regulates funeral directors and embalmers. The department can conduct in-person inspections without receiving a tip, but it is a complaint-driven agency and does not conduct periodic inspections on all facilities, according to the department.</p><p>Apparently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/10/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-oversight-illinois-decomposing-bodies" >no state agency oversees funeral homes themselves</a>, at their physical locations, officials said.</p><p>After the Chicago Heights Crematory case, Mendoza spearheaded <a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-susana-mendozas-legislation-strengthening-the-offices-oversight-of-crematoriums-signed-into-law" target="_blank" ><u>legislation</u></a> that gives the comptroller's office more investigative authority over crematories.</p><p>The bill authorizes the comptroller’s office to suspend a crematory license immediately in extreme cases and immediately do inspections after receiving a complaint, and it raises penalties to $10,000 per violation. The bill was signed into law this summer and takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation and the Illinois comptroller’s office have the authority to suspend and revoke licenses, impose fines and take other disciplinary measures. But according to that department, it doesn't have authority to bring criminal charges. Any suspected criminal activity would be investigated by law enforcement and charges would be brought by a state’s attorney.</p><h3>Are changes coming to oversight of the death care industry?</h3><p>In light of what happened at South Chicago Chapel, some legislators are talking about reforms. State Rep. Diane Blair-Sherlock, D-Villa Park, who co-sponsored the 2025 crematory legislation, said the state should consider putting funeral homes, crematories and licensing under a single authority. No bill has been proposed yet.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has questioned who should investigate funeral homes but has said little else about what kind of legislative response should follow.</p><h3>Have criminal charges been filed against South Chicago Chapel?</h3><p>Criminal charges haven’t been filed yet in spite of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" >demands from families</a> and people affected.</p><p>Chicago police are still investigating what happened at South Chicago Chapel. In August, the Cook County medical examiner’s office was still working to identify all the deceased, as well as the cremated remains of at least 56 more people.</p><p>In August, comptroller spokesperson Kim Howard said the office “referred our findings and met with the Cook County state’s attorney’s office and [Illinois State Police] in hopes of criminal charges being filed.”</p><p>Illinois State Police are still investigating the Chicago Heights crematory situation and are also assisting Chicago Police on the South Chicago Chapel investigation.</p><h3>What lawsuits have been filed against South Chicago Chapel?</h3><p>The city of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/08/31/clark-johanna-morgan-south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-lawsuit-building-department" >Chicago is suing the owners</a> of South Chicago Chapel for a litany of alleged building code violations, including the failure to keep buildings “clean, sanitary, and safe.” The city is asking a judge to issue a fine of $11,500 per day for every day the violations are not corrected.</p><p>The Morgans have been summoned to the first hearing of the Buildings Department’s lawsuit on Sept. 24 in Cook County Circuit Court.</p><p>In addition, a Texas woman launched a potential <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" ><u>class-action lawsuit</u></a> in August, alleging South Chicago Chapel mishandled the remains of her father along with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>dozens of other bodies</u></a>.</p><h3>Is the way Illinois regulates funeral homes unusual?</h3><p>Yes. Illinois is one of four states — along with Alaska, Hawaii and Iowa — that does not conduct any inspections of licensed funeral homes, crematories or cemeteries, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://theconferenceonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Regulations-in-Licensing-2025-Finalized.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>2025 survey</u></a> from the International Conference of Funeral Service Examining Boards.</p><p>A vast majority of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/south-deering-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-illinois-lax-oversight-inspections" ><u>other states carry out annual or biannual inspections</u></a> of funeral homes and sometimes even unannounced visits.</p><p>Illinois also is the only state that does not have a board or agency monitoring licensed funeral homes at their physical locations.</p><p>Thirty-six states have separate funeral boards to manage director licenses, funeral homes, crematories and cemeteries. The other states, excluding Illinois, have appointed state agencies, such as public health departments, to the task.</p><h3>Does the city of Chicago regulate funeral homes?</h3><p>Not directly. If a funeral home sells products, such as caskets or flowers, they must obtain a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" ><u>business license</u></a> issued by the Chicago Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection.</p><p>South Chicago Chapel does not have a Chicago business license, said a spokesperson for that department.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule entries.title: Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms return to Chicago this fall at Wrightwood 659
entries.summary: <p>On the second floor of Wrightwood 659, sits a portal to another world. Or, rather, two portals.</p><p>The boutique art museum in Lincoln Park is currently displaying two Infinity Mirror Rooms, the colorful, reflective and immersive artworks from the wildly popular Japanese artist <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/1102916697/yayoi-kusama-high-priestess-of-polka-dots-has-died" target="_blank" ><u>Yayoi Kusama</u></a>, who died in August at the age of 97.</p><p>The show at Wrightwood, “<a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/inner-worlds-visions-from-the-hirshhorn-collection/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24232358838&gbraid=0AAAAA9gf_bcO6dLEl_E7okwTCkd_IIrIY&gclid=Cj0KCQjw8c3VBhCsARIsAA_xJ92mjTrP4vNBtlLPmzYr_oHNQwDYfboVPaG0ahvKrWf-w6GXWgjgl6AaAkmvEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u>Inner Worlds: Visions from the Hirshhorn Collection</u></a>,” opens Friday and runs through Dec. 19. It is currently the only place in Chicago to experience Kusama’s mirrored rooms. Local audiences may be familiar with Kusama’s work from Chicago’s WNDR Museum, which, before it closed for good this month, featured the infinity room titled “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagogallerynews.com/articles/wndr-museum-announces-redesigned-yayoi-kusma-space-and-new-lounge-in-west-loop" target="_blank" ><u>LOVE IS CALLING</u></a>.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Inner Worlds: Visions from the Hirshhorn Collection</h3><br><b>When:</b> Sept. 25-Dec. 19<br><b>Where:</b> Wrightwood 659, 659 W. Wrightwood Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $20<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/inner-worlds-visions-from-the-hirshhorn-collection/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24232358838&gbraid=0AAAAA9gf_bcO6dLEl_E7okwTCkd_IIrIY&gclid=Cj0KCQjw8c3VBhCsARIsAA_xJ92mjTrP4vNBtlLPmzYr_oHNQwDYfboVPaG0ahvKrWf-w6GXWgjgl6AaAkmvEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >wrightwood659.org</a></div> </div><p>While Kusama developed the Infinity Mirror Rooms for decades — in fact, the show at Wrightwood features her first from 1965 — they had a resurgence in widespread popularity beginning in 2017, when the exhibit, “Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors,” toured the country. The show drew <a class="Link" href="https://www.si.edu/newsdesk/releases/hirshhorn-s-yayoi-kusama-infinity-mirrors-breaks-records" target="_blank" ><u>record attendance levels</u></a> at several museums and generated tremendous internet buzz, with visitors posting their mirrored art selfies to Instagram.</p><p>The moment helped to solidify Kusama’s place not only in art history, but also in pop culture. It led to her personal appearance — a blunt red bob and colorful dresses with geometric patterns — becoming as instantly recognizable as the polka dots and pumpkins often featured in her work.</p><p>But those bright colored motifs were pulled from Kusama’s own internal struggles. Throughout her life, the avant-garde artist talked openly about experiencing hallucinations, which began when she was a young child and led her to art. She also lived voluntarily at a psychiatric facility in Tokyo from the 1970s until her death.</p><p>That 2017 exhibit was organized by the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, the Smithsonian’s modern and contemporary art museum, which also curated the show at Wrightwood.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Yayoi Kusama’s “Pumpkin” is one of three of the artists iconic works presented in the exhibit.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Urquhart/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the new show, three of Kusama’s iconic works — two mirrored rooms and one large pumpkin sculpture — are presented alongside two of her art peers, Mary Bauermeister and Niki de Saint Phalle. Each of the women was a trailblazing 20th-century artist who forged careers at a time when the art world was still overwhelmingly male-dominated.</p><p>Plus, each of the women explored their own inner worlds and thought about how to immerse audiences in their work, including Bauermeister’s optical boxes, two of which are featured in the show and require a viewer to peer through a lens to catch sight of the drawing beneath.</p><p>Shown together, it allows audiences to understand Kusama’s work in the context of what else was happening in the art world throughout the 1950s and ’60s, a period in which all three of the women lived in New York. And already the Chicago show is attracting attention; Wrightwood staff say it is the most preregistrations they have ever had for an exhibition.</p><p>“People know Kusama really well, but we said it would be really great to spread out and look at who else was doing this,” said curator Betsy Johnson, who works at the Hirshhorn. “Who have [people] maybe not heard of yet? Who can we put in Kusama's company? And it very quickly came to the fore that Niki de Saint-Phalle and Mary Bauermeister were just such a good fit.”</p><p>While Kusama reached certified superstar status in her later years of life, she was not without controversy. After her death in August, <a class="Link" href="https://www.hawaiipublicradio.org/local-news/2026-09-10/japanese-artist-yayoi-kusama-death-revives-history-of-racist-remarks" target="_blank" ><u>racist anti-Black comments</u></a> she wrote in her autobiography resurfaced. Vice’s Dexter Thomas pointed out <a class="Link" href="https://www.vice.com/en/article/japans-most-famous-avant-garde-artist-banned-us-from-her-studio/" target="_blank" ><u>in 2017</u></a> that that section was removed from the English-language translation of the text. Thomas, who is Black, also reported on being banned from Kusama’s studio.</p><p>Kusama issued an apology in 2023, saying in a statement to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.sfchronicle.com/entertainment/article/yayoi-kusama-sfmoma-apology-18424518.php" target="_blank" ><u>San Francisco Chronicle</u></a>, “I deeply regret using hurtful and offensive language in my book. My message has always been one of love, hope, compassion, and respect for all people. My lifelong intention has been to lift up humanity through my art. I apologize for the pain I have caused.”</p><p>Johnson, who pointed both to Kusama’s ongoing mental illness and upbringing in a homogeneous culture, said the new Wrightwood exhibit does not directly address Kusama’s past comments.</p><p>“We definitely come upon these very unique individuals who may have mental illness, as Kusama did, and so their interactions with society are maybe not always along the same lines as one would hope,” Johnson said. “I think, in addition to her mental illness, there were probably also cultural conditions that were probably more challenging for her, but I do know that she did apologize, later in life, for making racist comments.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a previous shows included a 2018 display of Ai Weiwei’s “<a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/alphawood-gallery-ai-weiweis-trace-in-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>TRACE</u></a>” and a 2022 show called “<a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/rirkrit-tiravanija-whos-afraid-of-red-yellow-and-green-2/" target="_blank" ><u>Rirkrit Tiravanija: (who’s afraid of red, yellow, and green)</u></a>.”</p><p>The museum, which is privately owned by prominent philanthropist and Democratic megadonor Fred Eychaner, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2024/11/20/fred-eychaner-art-exhibit-wrightwood-659-chicago-gallery" target="_blank" ><u>sits along a residential block</u></a>, in a building that was reimagined by the renowned architect Tadao Ando. The museum has been looking to expand its footprint recently, but faces a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/museums/2026/06/08/wrightwood-659-lawsuit-lincoln-park-museum-fred-eychaner-art-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>court challenge </u></a>in doing so.</p><p>Still, due to its ownership model, the museum has been able to take <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2025/05/01/the-first-homosexuals-exhibit-wrightwood-695-chicago-museum" target="_blank" ><u>bolder swings</u></a> at a time when many museums are facing pressures, like the Smithsonian, which has been scrutinized by the Trump administration. Earlier this month, Lonnie Bunch III announced he will<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-and-culture/2026/09/08/lonnie-bunch-iii-resign-smithsonian-2026-trump-historian-chicago" target="_blank" ><u> step down as the head of the Smithsonian</u></a>. Amid his tenure, he tried to maintain the museum’s independence amid an internal review of the Smithsonian initiated by the administration <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/08/letter-to-the-smithsonian-internal-review-of-smithsonian-exhibitions-and-materials/" target="_blank" ><u>“to assess tone, historical framing, and alignment with American ideals</u></a>.”</p><p>Johnson said working with Wrightwood is a welcome chance to show off pieces of the Hirshhorn’s collection and bring the work to a Midwestern audience.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3f0000" name="image-3f0000"></a> <picture </div><p>“They really seem to be very driven to be showcasing artists with voices advocating for change and advocating for the greater good, and I think that's really amazing,” Johnson said.</p><p>Also on view at Wrightwood this fall is Taiwanese artist Yuan Goang-Ming’s show, “<a class="Link" href="https://wrightwood659.org/exhibitions/everyday-war-yuan-goang-ming/" target="_blank" ><u>Everyday War</u></a>,” an immersive, large-scale video installation, adapted from work shown at the Venice Biennale in 2024.</p><p>For Johnson, stepping into one of Kusama’s expansive mirrored rooms is like crossing a threshold into a world with seemingly no limits in sight.</p><p>“You just have a heightened awareness, which is something that I think we all crave. entries.title: Lil Rel on why he chose Chicago for his new comedy special
entries.summary: <p>Comedian Lil Rel Howery has come a long way from Chicago’s West Side and from his early days as a standup comic here. But lately, he’s spent a lot of time on screen, with credits that include a role in Jordan Peele’s Academy Award-winning film “Get Out,” NBC’s “The Carmichael Show” and even his own sitcom, “Rel,” on FOX.</p><p>Now, he’s coming home. Last weekend, Howery filmed his latest standup special at Black Ensemble Theatre. The homecoming show is part of the <a class="Link" href="https://events.eventnoire.com/profile/whats-funny-comedy" target="_blank" ><u>What’s Funny Comedy Festival</u></a>, running through Sept. 26, which Howery cofounded with his former manager Knowledge Beckom.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" I'm really hoping to build a relationship with them beyond just this special.”</p><p>Beckom said the festival came about organically. The fest will honor legend Bill Bellamy with the 2026 Icon Award.</p><p>“We want a blended festival,” said Beckom. “I don’t want 90% men. I want women comics. Chicago's always been the market to show people who's up next.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-740000" name="image-740000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9de8177/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F66%2F8c2e45fb4fa19058006163a17553%2Flilrel-260919-03.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6a33f79/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F66%2F8c2e45fb4fa19058006163a17553%2Flilrel-260919-03.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0bb1def/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F25%2F66%2F8c2e45fb4fa19058006163a17553%2Flilrel-260919-03.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Knowledge Beckom at the Chicago Public Media office at 848 E Grand Ave at Navy Pier, Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. About 40% of people performing this year are from out of town. We’re looking at them beyond just being funny on stage, but who looks like they have a story to tell?”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even with the heavy crop of talent traveling for the festival, the headline event will be the taping of Howery’s new special. And the content of his performance will hit close to home.</p><p>“My dad passed in January, and while I was planning the funeral, comedy kept showing up,” he said. “I told my brother after the funeral, ‘I want to do a special dedicated to dad.’ Everything I'm doing the next few weeks in Chicago — the comedy festival, and I’m shooting a limited series that I wrote and created — it's a love letter to my family. It's my love letter to Chicago and to the way I grew up.”</p><p>Chicago has established itself as a premier destination for comedy and for standups, specifically Black standups. The city's clubs provide a fertile training ground where many notable comics earned their stripes.</p><p>“People get mad when we say this, but the best comedians come out of Chicago,” said Howery. “And the reason, I believe, is because of how segregated Chicago is. You have to know how to make so many different people laugh in this city, and not just Black people. Once you figure out that I can go to any spot in the city and make people laugh. … Chicago did this for me — I was able to be so confident coming to L.A. and going to New York because Chicago made me feel like a star already.”</p><p> Howery also gives a nod to a local legend on building confidence.</p><p>“Think about Bernie Mac,” he said. “For us Black comics, he set the tone for what being yourself looks like. And in Chicago we’re all comfortable in our own skin. That's what makes us great comedians.” </p><p>These days, Howery lives in Los Angeles. But when he comes home, he likes to spend time in his old neighborhood.</p><p> “I like just driving up and down Madison. I did it yesterday. I do it every time I show up to Chicago,” he said. “It's so many different parts of memories. If I drive to Western, I remember going to the laundromat on Saturdays with my mother, me and my brothers carrying our stuff. If I keep going further down, I see Providence St. Mel. My parents sacrificed to make sure I went to a better school. They didn't even have it like that.”</p><p>He also makes a few unusual stops. Lately, he’s found himself stopping by the funeral home where his family held services when his father died.</p><p>“This gonna sound crazy,” he said. “I just wanted to stop there. I know he’s not there, but I built a relationship because I was there so much. You know how weird it is for me to just be there with some other people's family?”</p><p>He continued: “I love what Chicago represents for me. I was driving up and down out west the other day and stopped to get some snowballs, and they was like, ‘Lil Rel what you doing on Central Park?’ And because they recognized me, I felt like I had to buy everybody snowballs, so I did.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-870000" name="image-870000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/101b017/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cf4aec6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf59d2f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lil Rel Howery at the Chicago Public Media office at 848 E Grand Ave at Navy Pier, Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf59d2f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9adb6e0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf59d2f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F70%2F6e%2Ffe68ba044cbd81eb1a10d5def2fe%2Flilrel-260919-20.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“I was able to be so confident coming to L.A. and going to New York because Chicago made me feel like a star already,” Howery said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Howery has always maintained a close connection to the city, even after work took him away. When he filmed his sitcom, “Rel,” on FOX, the theme song was homegrown.</p><p>“One of my favorite songs is Crucial Conflict’s ‘In The Circle,’” he said, “because we all used to hang out in the circle, you know, on Madison and Central Park. It’s crazy, but I’m one of those lunatics. I said if I ever have a show that will be the theme song. So I had FOX call them, and pay them to remake it into a theme song.”</p><p>Looking forward to the festival, Howery said he’s eager for a chance to see the new crop of talented comedians.</p><p>“Chicago's just a great place for standup comedy,” said Howery. “And not only standup. Like legendary sketch actors also come from Chicago. Every part of comedy, the best have come from here.”</p>
