entries.title: Option attack lifts improving St. Ignatius into Super 25 rankings
entries.summary: <p>As more teams in the Catholic League shift toward spread offenses, St. Ignatius has stayed true to its triple-option attack under coach Matt Miller.</p><p>The Wolfpack missed the IHSA playoffs each of the last two years, but Miller and his program slowly built momentum back with a pair of Prep Bowl championships. Those championships set the table for a resurgent 2026 season. Behind players like Nino Capuano and Reid Hites, St. Ignatius has improved more than arguably any Catholic League team.</p><p>“We knew that we were very talented and we could go really far,” Capuano, a sophomore, said. “If you’re looking from an outside perspective as a fan or other teams, I feel like a lot of people doubted us thinking we were going to be the same Ignatius from the past two years.</p><p>Playoff-bound for the first time since 2023, St. Ignatius (4-1, 1-0 CCL Orange) has already doubled its regular-season win total from a year ago. The Wolfpack have beaten quality opponents too, defeating defending Class 6A champion Fenwick and Class 7A finalist St. Rita. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/20/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >St. Ignatius joined the Super 25 rankings on Sunday.</a></p><p>St. Ignatius is averaging 39.2 points per game through five weeks, nearly twice its scoring number from last season.</p><p>“We’re in a position that I thought we would be,” Miller said. “We expected to be in this spot competing for a division title, so I wouldn’t say it’s a surprise. That’s been the goal of our players. We want to win a state championship regardless of what class we’re in.”</p><p>Capuano set a new school record for rushing yards against St. Rita. The 5-7, 180-pounder erupted for 279 yards and three scores in a 42-16 victory.</p><p>“My field vision has gotten a lot better,” Capuano said. “I went to a lot of camps to get better at my position. I’ve made a huge all-around jump in running the ball.”</p><p>Hites, meanwhile, has captained the St. Ignatius offense since he returned from elbow surgery late in his sophomore year. The junior quarterback accounted for six touchdowns in only 8.5 quarters of work over the team’s first three games this year.</p><p>Hites’ older brother Connor is a key factor on the Wolfpack defense at safety. He intercepted two passes, made two sacks and totaled 10 tackles against Hope Academy. He then helped contain Iowa recruit Jake Thies in the 30-20 win over Fenwick, recording 12 tackles, one sack and one forced fumble.</p><p>St. Ignatius’ only loss came against unbeaten IC Catholic and the Wolfpack has allowed just 64 points in five games. The win over Fenwick was St. Ignatius’s first divisional victory since 2023, when the Wolfpack won the Green with a 3-0 mark.</p><p>“Our connection this year is a lot stronger than it’s been in years past,” Reid Hites said. “Our goals are a lot bigger and I feel like we had a different mentality going into the season. We don’t want to be overlooked anymore and I feel like our work has paid off so far...With the Fenwick game and the Rita game, we went into those games overlooked, but from within, everyone on the team knew we could win those games. That was the ultimate goal and we did that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage at Friday Night Drive.</a></p>
entries.author: Russ Hodges

entries.title: Dual-threat quarterback Will Clark has kept Fremd on the winning track
entries.summary: <p>Will Clark had a hard act to follow at Fremd.</p><p>Last year as a sophomore, Clark was the backup to Vikings quarterback Johnny O'Brien. Now at Northwestern, O'Brien was a three-year starter who piled up 8.395 total yards and 93 touchdowns in his prep career.</p><p>No surprise, O'Brien got virtually all the practice reps. But when he missed a Week 7 game at Barrington with an injury, Clark was pressed into action for his first varsity start.</p><p>Barrington won 23-7 and Clark was 9 of 19 passing for 156 yards. But he learned some valuable lessons that are paying off this season.</p><p>With Clark as the starter this year, Fremd is 4-1. Through the first five games of the season, Clark had thrown for 1,081 yards with three TDs.</p><p>"Ever since that [Barrington loss], I've had ... this chip on my shoulder to do a lot better," Clark told the Sun-Times. "And I'd say that my preparation is a lot different now for each game. I feel like last year, sometimes I got off track. But this year I've been very focused and learning a lot of things from the coaches."</p><p>He also picked up plenty from watching O'Brien on and off the field.</p><p>"I learned a lot from him," Clark said. "Like ... you have to watch your film. You have to know what the defense is doing at all times. And then in actual game situations — reading the defense and your footwork and everything, I learned a lot from that."</p><p>O'Brien is 6-3 and 200 pounds, 3 inches taller and 30 pounds heavier than Clark, so it's no surprise they have different profiles.</p><p>Clark is being used as more of a dual-threat quarterback than O'Brien.</p><p>"He's had some longer runs," Fremd coach Lou Sponsel said of Clark. "He's had some designed runs. Like Week 1, [Lake Zurich was] overshifting to take away some of our stuff in the pass game so we let Will run our zone game into the boundaries.</p><p>"And Johnny could have run, too. We just said, no, we're not running Johnny."</p><p>Meanwhile, Sponsel said Clark is developing as a pocket passer. "But he's still got that dual threat to where he can scramble. He can run at any time, either as a designed quarterback run or he just takes off and runs," Sponsel said.</p><p>Clark is comfortable in either phase of the game.</p><p>"I've always liked to use my feet whenever I get the chance to," he said. "And I also love chucking the ball down the field and making plays doing that."</p><p>Even if he wasn't following in the footsteps of a Power Four recruit, Clark knew he'd be in the spotlight as the starting quarterback for a high-profile program. Win or lose, taking heat or praise, he lets it roll off his back.</p><p>"I always stay away from that," he said of the outside noise. "I don't pay attention to that at all. I always move on from it, next play mentality, next game mentality."</p><p>Similarly, during the school year and the summer, Clark toggles back and forth between two sports: football and baseball. He also played basketball, but gave it up after eighth grade.</p><p>"When it comes to baseball and football, sometimes when I need a break from one of them I always just go to the next," he said.</p><p>For now, though, he's enjoying this football ride.</p>

entries.title: Man, 18, accused of fatally stabbing woman, 18, in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old man is accused of fatally stabbing an 18-year-old woman to death early Tuesday in Englewood.</p><p>Alfredo Tzoy, 18, was charged with murder and was scheduled to appear for a detention hearing Thursday.</p><p>Tzoy, of the Englewood neighborhood, was arrested shortly after the attack, which left the still-unidentified 18-year-old woman dead, police and the Cook County medical examiner’s office said.</p><p>She was found on the ground in the 7300 block of South Emerald Avenue, with a stab wound to the neck. She was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Officers searching the area discovered Tzoy on a nearby porch with a cut to his right hand, police said.</p><p>A knife was recovered. </p>

Chicago</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjjtlkk-l-tj/" target="_blank" >Maggie Hennessy</a></h5><p>More than a century after Wrigley, Brach's and Mars helped turn Chicago into a candy epicenter, a trio of artists with an unabashed candy obsession brought their gummy candy startup to the shuttered former Jelly Belly plant in suburban North Chicago, ushering in a new era for this storied city of sweets production.</p><p>The actor Martin Starr and musicians and twins Ezra and Adeev Potash cofounded Sweet Stash last fall with an additive-free gummy with the complex flavor and texture dimension of candies they discovered over years of globe-trekking.</p><p>"We are obsessed with candy beyond what's normal and maybe even healthy," Ezra said.</p><p>After months of routinely selling out on Amazon amid requests from retailers for their toothsome, musical note-shaped Jams gummies in flavors like Prickly Pear, Strawbarb and White Peach, the company moved production from Nebraska (the twins' home state) to Ferrara's 113-year-old Jelly Belly factory in April.</p><p>The move doesn't just mean taking on bigger orders and getting onto more indie store shelves while maintaining consistency in a product free from gluten, synthetic dyes and corn syrup. This self-starting trio can also keep making candy limited mostly by their imaginations in a city known for confectionery innovation — a rarity for an industry dominated by profit-seeking conglomerates.</p><p>"We're a small band of creative people going up against billion-dollar companies that make candy by the tank," Adeev said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjjtlkk-l-tt/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><h4></h4><p><b>Aside from the ballpark, where's the next best place to watch a Cubs or White Sox game? entries.title: CSO’s parent organization rebrands as “Chicago Symphony”
entries.summary: <p>The nonprofit parent organization of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra announced a rebrand Thursday, meant to usher in a new era for the city’s preeminent classical music company. It features a new naming convention and, for the first time in 30 years, a new logo.</p><p>Music fans will also notice updated red uniforms for the ushers who greet and seat guests. And while the rest of the changes are mostly subtle from the audience perspective, company leaders say the rebrand is meant to clarify the organization’s identity and is part of a broader strategy to attract younger, more diverse audiences.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" data-module entries.title: Bulls announce rotation of TV analysts to replace the late Stacey King
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls announced their local-TV broadcast plans for the season Thursday, including a rotation of analysts who will share the job of replacing the late Stacey King. </p><p>Play-by-play voice Adam Amin will be joined by Kendall Gill, Robbie Hummel, Will Perdue, Bill Wennington and Scott Williams. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/03/kendall-gill-will-perdue-scott-williams-robbie-hummel-chicago-bulls-tv-analyst-stacey-king" target="_blank" >The Sun-Times had reported</a> this month on the Bulls' plan to rotate analysts. Since then, radio analyst Wennington was added to the group.</p><p>King, who died June 7 at his home in River Forest, had been the Bulls’ TV analyst for 20 years, entertaining fans with his humor, wit and trademark sayings. The Bulls think a rotation will ease the pressure on the analysts and serve as an audition for the permanent job.</p><p>Gill also will be on the Chicago Sports Network studio team with host Cam Smith and reporter K.C. Johnson. CHSN will air all five Bulls preseason games and 80 regular-season games. All home games will be available in 4K. </p><p>Bulls radio voice Chuck Swirsky and Wennington return to call games on The Score, which will carry three preseason games and every regular-season and postseason game. Alyssa Bergamini returns to host the station’s postgame show.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Illinois Supreme Court hears arguments in fight over Chicago police disciplinary process
entries.summary: <p>Lawyers for the city and its largest police union faced off Thursday morning before the Illinois Supreme Court, arguing over the handling of disciplinary hearings for officers accused of egregious misconduct. </p><p>The arguments marked the latest chapter of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >yearslong legal battle</a> that snaked its way from the union bargaining table to City Council and now all levels of state court, halting Chicago’s police oversight system in the process.</p><p>Last year, a panel of appellate judges ruled officers could have disciplinary cases heard by an arbitrator, instead of the Chicago Police Board. But the appeals court also ruled that hearings must remain <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/08/08/chicago-police-cpd-misconduct-discipline-arbitration-ruling-appellate-court" target="_blank" >open to the public</a>, prompting the police union's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline" target="_blank" >appeal to the state Supreme Court</a>.</p><p>In Springfield Thursday, Matt Pierce, a lawyer for the Fraternal Order of Police, said there’s no statute or public policy requiring labor proceedings be open to the public, and that those hearings are "inherently private” </p><p>“The city is effectively taking this very broad, almost aspirational policy behind statutes … and suggesting that those very broad blanket statements of transparency and accountability require certain hearings to be held in public,” Pierce said.</p><p>One Supreme Court justice asked Pierce whether the federal consent decree mandating sweeping Chicago police reforms is policy, as argued by Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul in a brief to the court. </p><p>“It certainly may be the case that consent decree incorporates and references existing public policy … but it does not serve as a basis to create public policy,” Pierce responded. “If a document like a consent decree can establish the public policy for the entire state of Illinois that means two parties can set policies that are binding on an entire state.”</p><p>Another justice questioned whether ruling on this disagreement between the city and its largest police union would have effects on other jurisdictions that may already have private arbitration.</p><p>“This is a public policy that could apply anywhere,” said Aya Barnea, a city lawyer. “But whether it applies … depends on context.” </p><p>“Chicago’s facts matter – the fact that we’ve done it this way for 60 years, the fact that in Chicago it is just a reality that there is a deep distrust among many members of the community of the police department,” Barnea added.</p><p>Community members want to know if the office they’re calling to their home is “a person of integrity,” Barnea said. “It’s important that the public have confidence in the police department and having these hearings be public is a key piece of building that public confidence,” she said.</p><p>Union president John Catanzara said the decision before the justices is “pretty clear.”</p><p>“If you strictly are there to interpret the law as written … there is really no decision other than enforcing the arbitration award as written,” Catanzara told the Sun-Times after court.</p><p>He said the issue of other jurisdictions has always been a hurdle the city “could never clear.”</p><p>“This never had the ability to be segregated to just Chicago because of Illinois labor laws,” Catanzara said. “They wanted it to be just Chicago but that's not the reality.”</p><p>The court is also primed to rule on whether officers who face firing must still be paid while their cases are pending. The appellate court sided with the union in finding those officers should remain on the city payroll.</p><p>Barnea argued for the state Supreme Court to overturn that portion of the appellate court ruling, claiming it was “arbitrary and capricious.”</p><p>“If the award stands, the city will be forced to pay officers that the superintendent does not believe should perform any police duties, and it places unfair financial burdens on taxpayers,” Barnea added.</p><p>The state Supreme Court typically issues opinions a few months after oral arguments, according to a spokeswoman for the court.</p><p>Regardless of the outcome, the police board is urging officers not to seek arbitration and proceed with their cases before the board.</p><p>Even after a ruling is released, the city and police union will still have to work to establish an arbitration process,contributing to further delays.</p><p>The board, on the other hand, is “ready and able to hear disciplinary cases,” according to Kyle Cooper, the police board president. </p><p>“This delay serves no one,” Cooper said last month. “Officers should not have to spend years with serious charges hanging over them. Alleged victims should not have to wait years for resolution.”</p><p>So far, only four of the 31 officers currently facing charges have elected to have their cases heard by the police board. The other 27 cases remain in limbo as officers await the state Supreme Court’s ruling.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/09/23/chicago-police-misconduct-supreme-court" target="_blank" >https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/09/16/chicago-police-union-fop-misconduct-discipline</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/08/08/chicago-police-cpd-misconduct-discipline-arbitration-ruling-appellate-court" target="_blank" >Chicago cops accused of serious misconduct must face public hearings, appeals court rules</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/03/21/chicago-cops-serious-discipline-arbitrator-public" target="_blank" >Chicago cops facing serious discipline can take cases to arbitrator, but judge says hearings should be public</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: CATCH-22: Scouting the challenges for Bears' starting QB
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Dan Orlvosky (1)</b>, the ESPN analyst who came off the bench more than he started as an NFL quarterback. Just because the backup quarterback is the most popular player in any city, he told me, doesn’t make it an easy job.</p><p>“Everyone thinks backup quarterback is the greatest job in the world, and there’s a lot of good to it,” he said. “But you do a lot of work with no payoff. Yes, it’s your job. But the competitive payoff, the professional pride payoff, you don’t get. And when the opportunity presents itself, it’s very rare.”</p><p>That’s what makes this week so compelling for both <b>Tyson Bagent</b> <b>(2)</b> and <b>Case Keenum (3)</b>.</p><p>After <b>Caleb Williams</b> <b>(4)</b> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/23/case-keenum-the-only-active-bears-qb-to-practice-wednesday" target="_blank" >pulled his hamstring</a>, Bagent thought he had a long-awaited starting opportunity. His contract expires at the end of next year, and a good stint with the starters would raise his future value. Bagent reported concussion symptoms on Tuesday, though, two days after relieving Williams in the fourth quarter. Every passing day lessens the odds he’ll play against the Eagles.</p><p>“You have the thought of, ‘I’m working so hard for this very moment,’” Orlovsky said. “Everyone always told me, ‘Just be ready — you never know when your opportunity is going to come.’ You get it, if you’re Tyson, on a team that you can probably go operate well and continue to make a name and future for yourself …</p><p>“If he’s unable to go because of [the concussion] it’s disappointing.”</p><p>Enter Keenum, who is 38 and hasn’t started since 2023.</p><p>“I’m 43 and I have no idea how guys like <b>Tom Brady</b> <b>(5)</b> did it, I have no idea how a guy like <b>Aaron Rodgers</b> <b>(6)</b> is still playing,” Orlovsky said. “Thirty-eight is not that far off."</p><p>Orlvosky listed three challenges for a backup thrust into the starting role. It starts with game speed — even the crispest practice operates at about 70% of that pace, he said. Scout team quarterbacks take risks under the pretense of testing their own starting defense, and that attitude has to shift on game day. Finally, situational football — third downs, short yardage, and late-game work — requires drilling backups don’t often get.</p><p>Keenum has that experience, even if it’s been years since he’s used it in a game.</p><p>“That’s why you keep a guy like that around,” Orlovsky said.</p><h3><b>The Bears’ only other healthy QB is …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Miller Moss (7), </b>the<b> </b>rookie the Bears cut after training camp. Moss went home to Pacific Palisades, Calif., and wasn’t quite sure what do to.</p><p>“For lack a better word,” he said, “I was sitting around, working out and hoping the phone was going to ring.”</p><p>When it did, it was the Bears. Bagent’s back spasms leading to the season opener prompted the Bears to fly him out two days before the opener, sign him to the practice squad the next day and use him as their emergency quarterback. He hasn't been home since.</p><p>Monday, he could be one rolled ankle away from playing.</p><p>Crazy, right?</p><p>“I think getting caught up in possible eventualities is a slippery slope,” he said, “especially with what I’ve seen in the last 12 days.”</p><h3><b>Now that’s a grizzly Bear …</b></h3><p><b>Marcedes Lewis</b> <b>(8)</b>, the tight end who played his age 40 season in 2024, is the oldest Bear to appear in a game. Not counting specialists, quarterback <b>Todd Collins</b> <b>(9)</b>, tackle <b>Jason Peters</b> <b>(10)</b> and Lewis are the only Bears to play their age 39 season.</p><p>Only four non-specialists played their age 38 season, and they’re all quarterbacks. <b>Chris Chandler (11)</b> went 3-3 as the starter in 2003 and <b>Dave Krieg</b> (12) went 6-6 in 1996. <b>Rudy Bukich</b> <b>(13)</b> threw seven passes off the bench in 1968.</p><p>Then there’s <b>Greg Landry</b> <b>(14)</b>, a 14-year NFL vet the Bears pulled out of retirement to play the 1984 regular season finale with <b>Jim McMahon</b> <b>(15)</b> and <b>Steve Fuller</b> <b>(16)</b> hurt. Quarterback<b> Rusty Lisch</b> <b>(17)</b> was so bad the week before that <b>Mike Ditka</b> <b>(18)</b> benched him — for running back <b>Walter Payton (19)</b>.</p><p>Two days before he turned 38 — which counts as 38 in the NFL’s record-keeping — Landry beat his former team, the Lions. Fuller returned for the playoffs, eventually losing to the 49ers in an NFC title game that motivated Ditka during the next year’s Super Bowl run.</p><p>Landry, who played for the USFL’s Chicago Blitz a year before his Bears cameo, later served as the Bears’ offensive coordinator from 1988-92.</p><h3><b>At least I had the winner right …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Robert Griffin III</b> <b>(20)</b> and <b>Andrew Luck</b> <b>(21)</b> were the top two players I submitted on my 2011 Heisman Trophy ballot, and they finished in that order. My third-place vote went to Keenum, who set the NCAA’s career passing record — one that, amazingly, still stands —at Houston. He finished seventh.</p><h3><b>Thank God it wasn’t Casual Friday …</b></h3><p><b>Jahdae Walker (22)</b>, the most boisterous Bear, wore a collared Nike Dri-Fit golf shirt under his practice pads two days before the Vikings game.</p><p>“Business Friday,” he said.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: The young know artificial intelligence is 'going to be part of our lives for a really, really long time'
entries.summary: <p>Robots, rather than the software that runs them, are what first appealed to Soham Batra.</p><p>"My interest in technology didn't start with AI," said the 17-year old high school senior. "It started with robotics. When I was a lot younger, around elementary school, I was very involved with Lego robotics. That sparked my interest. I was thrown into a class where we expected to make them move. We're just a bunch of 6-year-olds and I was [thinking]: 'How do I even do that?' Then I started looking into it and found programming, coding. As I moved to high school the entire AI bubble started expanding, and got to everyone."</p><p>High school for Batra being the Illinois Math and Science Academy (IMSA) in Aurora, a residential hive of some of the brightest kids in the state. There the senior distinguished himself... well, maybe we should let him explain, the way he did in his introductory email:</p><p>"You wrote last year that the AI genie is out of the bottle. I'm one of the people crawling into the bottle after it, and I'm in high school," he began. "I do machine learning research on the side. Two of my papers were oral presentations at ICML and CVPR 2026 workshops (one on keeping a model aligned while it keeps learning, one on carrying 3D reconstruction uncertainty into physics simulations)..."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2d0000" name="module-2d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>ICML is the International Conference on Machine Learning. CVPR refers to the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. Before we wander too far into the weeds, I should explain why I was interested in Batra.</p><p>Most everything I see in the press about artificial intelligence is disaster-oriented. The leaders of AI, sounding the gong of doom. But kids like Batra don't see it that way. To him, AI is just "a really cool tool."</p><p>"The thing with AI, there's nothing like it," he said. "I got really lucky, to see the development of AI at a very young age. A lot of people ask if the AI bubble is going to pop... If you try to do your day-to-day tasks without AI, and with AI — you'll really see a really big difference."</p><p>At IMSA, students are given Wednesdays off to tend to side projects, and I could fill the column with Batra's — such as doing research at the University of Chicago's Booth School of Business.</p><p>The project that really impressed me, however, is a simulation he built called <a class="Link" href="https://nthchance.com/" target="_blank" >“Play the House,”</a> where participants run a casino, adding new games, setting the house edge, all the way down to dangling drink specials. Young people are being seduced into gambling, particularly at colleges, which abandon their responsibility to look out for their charges by allowing betting sites to entice them. The point of Batra's game, which he made in "an extremely basic version" before using AI to "glamour it up a bit so it was ready to put out there on a domain" is to drive home the insurmountable advantage casinos enjoy.</p><p>"I've had a couple family members succumb to gambling," he said. "I've seen what it can do, first-hand." He developed the game, "to better help people understand how the odds are stacked against them."</p><p>Space doesn't allow me to explain his AI work, not that I understand it myself.</p><p>"In my opinion, the most important [of his papers] he calls 'the geometry of forgetting,'" said his IMSA adviser, Steve Goldblatt. "When you are working with AI, machine learning, it is an iterative process. What he has done with that is brilliant. He found a way for those parameters — for what you put in to stay in through the entire iterative process."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5e0000" name="image-5e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eb6671f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6b0d6db/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/12ed1d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Soham Batra, an Illinois Math and Science Academy, senior and Steve Goldblatt, Program Manager of Entrepreneurship and Innovation, inside the school's 3D printing room on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/12ed1d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ef98a8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/12ed1d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3400x1908+0+138/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2Ff3%2F21fa1a92405798c7364a935df3e3%2Fsteinbergfridaysoham-260925-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Soham Batra, an Illinois Math and Science Academy, senior and Steve Goldblatt, the academy’s program manager of entrepreneurship and innovation, inside the school’s 3D printing room.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Mark Black/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Batra, who is from Naperville and whose parents are immigrants from India, is also the goaltender on the school's varsity soccer team.</p><p>"He's closer to your actual teenager than a lot of the students here," said Goldblatt. "He jokes around. Very social, has a lot of friends here. At IMSA, we have a student body of introverts. Soham is definitely an extrovert, out there talking to people."</p><p>When I asked why he reached out to me, his answer was surprising.</p><p>"Honestly, I always look for guidance in what I'm trying to do," Batra said. "Often time, the advice people give me doesn't exactly help me. What helps me is when people ask me questions about what I want to do. When I answer the questions, I figure out a lot more about what I actually want to do. It's something I think about often, but when people ask me, I'm able to give them an answer. I'm trying to figure out what I'm trying to do. Steps like these are important."</p> <p>For instance, I asked about his college plans. He thinks he will go, but two former classmates at IMSA went to college then immediately dropped out and formed companies now worth $90 million. The straight-to-business route is tempting.</p><p>While that decision looms, he is ironing out the future of AI, which does veer toward malfunction.</p><p>"You have to train models, so they're able to answer questions," he said. "When these big companies develop open AI, they train them on text, images. They have to have certain guidelines, to refuse harmful requests. That's what you call alignment. When you take that same AI and you fine tune it on something else, you  try to make the AI specific to medical records, or legal documents, the alignment shifts slightly and the safety behavior degrades. People are able to find slight loopholes when you over-train a model. It has something called a 'context window,' the amount of information it's able to handle. Once it exceeds that, it hallucinates, meaning it provides misinformation. My study was on how safety behavior degrades. how easy is it to degrade the safety model."</p><p>"I get the impression it's real easy," I said.</p><p>"It is kinda scary how easy it is," he said. "You can watch the alignment degrade. There's no exceptions to it not degrading. It's not possible to improve it. The only thing it can do is make it worse."</p><p>That sounds bad.</p><p>"The thing I did find, no matter how you fine tune, you could never get it to do something so terrible," Batra said. "The contributions, the strides we've made in AI, there's no way that it's not going to be part of our lives for a really, really long time. Almost forever. It is a very useful tool and should be consistently used, but more research should make it safer. It will be a lot more useful."</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks get cost certainty on Oliver Moore's new five-year contract
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> obtained a valuable bit of cost certainty in a very uncertain NHL salary-cap environment Thursday.</p><p>Second-year forward <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/20/blackhawks-oliver-moore-nick-lardis-depth-roles-training" >Oliver Moore</a> signed a five-year contract extension carrying a $4.25 million cap hit, which kicks in next summer after the final year of his current entry-level contract.</p><p>"What we have here is so special," Moore said. "I wish I could sign for 15 years."</p><p>From the Hawks' perspective, this represents a significant long-term commitment to a 21-year-old player with only 60 career games played, during which he has averaged less than 13 minutes of ice time per game and tallied a modest 23 points.</p><p>But those types of long-term commitments are becoming increasingly common around the league.</p><p>The Penguins signed 23-year-old forward Ville Koivunen, who has 14 points in 47 career games, to an eight-year contract with a $4 million cap hit earlier this summer, for example. And the Golden Knights signed 23-year-old forward Braeden Bowman, who has 26 points in 54 games, to a six-year contract with a $3.4 million cap hit earlier this month.</p><p>Moore's cap hit comes in slightly above Koivunen's and Bowman's cap hits, but as a former first-round pick who's two years younger than those two, there's good reason to believe his upside is higher.</p><p>"He's a puck hunter...[and] he's got that kind of intensity away from the puck," coach Jeff Blashill said. "I think he’s learning to have the calmness with the puck."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/20/blackhawks-oliver-moore-nick-lardis-depth-roles-training" >Oliver Moore, Nick Lardis could bolster Blackhawks’ depth with second-year leaps</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Moore's contract is arguably more comparable to the contract fellow Hawks forward Frank Nazar signed last summer, for six years with a roughly $6.6 million cap hit. Moore's cap hit comes in $2.35 million below that.</p><p>Even if Moore plateaus as a third-line specialist — a speedster who makes a difference in the defensive and neutral zones but lacks a strong finishing touch — the contract should still turn out to be reasonable. </p><p>The standard prices for different types of role players, after all, have been completely re-framed by the skyrocketing cap.</p><p>"When you have a guy like him who competes so hard and works so hard and is obviously as fast as he is, that can be an extremely dangerous weapon," Nazar said.</p><p>Nazar later interrupted Moore's interview scrum by tossing some $100 bills on his head, prompting a round of laughter. The two of them do tend to be the epicenter of silliness and fun inside the locker room.</p><p>"We believe in what [Oliver is] going to continue to build as a player," Blashill said, "but we also know he’s a huge part of our locker room. He probably gives [Connor Bedard] the most [crap], so that’s an important piece. He’s just got that in him."</p><p>Somehow, Moore managed to keep his negotiations secret from the rest of the team until Thursday morning, which is impressive considering how much of a talker he usually is. Nazar described that as a testament to Moore's humility.</p><p>"You just keep that stuff private," Moore said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Frank Nazar threw a bunch of $100 bills at Oliver Moore after his contract extension with Chicago 😂 <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/Blackhawks?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Blackhawks</a> <a href="https://t.co/P8btr1S8Cs">pic.twitter.com/P8btr1S8Cs</a></p>— Charlie Roumeliotis (@CRoumeliotis) <a href="https://x.com/CRoumeliotis/status/2103177440877031754?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Moore added he would like to get involved in community service around Chicago now that he can consider himself a permanent resident. He could pick up longtime defenseman Connor Murphy's torch on that front.</p><p>"Going to the firefighter station, the police department, the hospitals here are unbelievable," Moore said. "There are so many people around here that make this a safe and special city. I want to try to do stuff that way, for sure."</p><p>Hawks general manager Kyle Davidson could explore long-term extensions for other pending 2027 restricted free agents, too, now that a trend has been established.</p><p>Forwards Ryan Greene and Landon Slaggert and defensemen Artyom Levshunov, Sam Rinzel and Wyatt Kaiser all fall in that bucket.</p>

entries.title: Famed radio and TV priest Fulton Sheen to be beatified in St. Louis, a step away from sainthood
entries.summary: <p>Decades after he was a fixture on American TV screens, the late <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/fulton-sheen-catholic-peoria-illinois-beatification-da364dcb0ca25cd49c637bd3be85197b" target="_blank" >Archbishop Fulton Sheen</a> is back in a familiar place: the media spotlight.</p><p>Tens of thousands of Catholic devotees are converging on St. Louis for a formal ceremony of beatification on Thursday, in which the prelate will be designated Blessed Fulton Sheen — one step away from sainthood.</p><p>The afternoon ceremony is taking place at the Dome at America's Center after years of delays. The stadium was chosen for the site because there wasn't a venue large enough in his home Diocese of Peoria, Illinois, to accommodate the anticipated number of attendees.</p><p>About 50,000 tickets were distributed as of Thursday, according to organizers with the diocese and the Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen Foundation, which advocates for his sainthood. By early morning, the downtown streets were filling up with pilgrims, many of them priests in clerical garb and nuns in habits. Scores of bishops, a thousand priests and hundreds of religious order members, seminarians and deacons were expected.</p><p>A temporary altar was set up on the stage in the indoor stadium, backed by photos — including Sheen's tomb at the Peoria cathedral, now a destination for pilgrims.</p><p>The event honors a prelate who was once a regular presence in the living rooms of millions of Americans — including that of the future <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/pope-leo-xiv" target="_blank" >Pope Leo XIV</a>, who says he <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pope-leo-fulton-sheen-beatification-5d7402707f81d5a33dab18a82dff80ff" target="_blank" >watched the broadcasts</a> of his fellow Illinois native while growing up in Chicago.</p><h3>Sheen’s journey from Peoria to primetime</h3><p>Sheen was a pioneering radio priest who quickly adopted the new medium of television in the 1950s, when he began hosting the program, “Life is Worth Living.” Dressed in a cassock, cape and skullcap, he stood at a chalkboard and delivered moral and religious lessons without a narrow Catholic focus.</p><p>The show competed favorably against entertainers Milton Berle and Frank Sinatra on other networks. In an Emmy acceptance speech, Sheen thanked his writers — Gospel scribes Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. He’s been called America’s first televangelist.</p><p>“Archbishop Sheen was a beacon of faith, hope, and love who shone through radio and television for decades,” Pope Leo said in a June speech to directors of The Pontifical Mission Societies, which Sheen headed in the U.S. for 16 years. “I myself witnessed his evangelization efforts as I was growing up.”</p><p>Sheen was born in 1895 in the small town of El Paso, Illinois, and raised in Peoria. After becoming a priest and earning a doctorate in philosophy, he had a short pastorate in Peoria before becoming a professor at The Catholic University of America in Washington.</p><p>He became known both for his academic lectures and his plainspoken addresses from the pulpit and the studio, first on radio and then on TV. He often signed off with the benediction, “God love you.”</p><p>Sheen appeared in a Time magazine cover article. He guided celebrities and others converting to Catholicism.</p><p>He met with popes and spoke at the reformist Second Vatican Council. He railed against communism, though he opposed the Vietnam War.</p><p>Sheen raised funds and traveled the world on behalf of Catholic missions. He served as a bishop in New York state, retiring as an archbishop. After his death at 84, he was buried at St. Patrick’s Cathedral in New York until his niece won a court battle in 2019 to move his body to Peoria’s Cathedral of St. Mary of the Immaculate Conception.</p><h3>The Illinois teen tied to Sheen’s path to sainthood</h3><p>It's there, where Sheen had been a young altar server and was later ordained a priest, that pilgrims now place crucifixes and other items on his marble tomb, giving them status as relics.</p><p>To qualify for beatification, the Vatican normally requires one miracle attributable to the faithful seeking the candidate's heavenly prayers.</p><p>The late Pope Francis approved the beatification, attributing to Sheen the resuscitation of an infant born in 2010 without a pulse and revived only after lengthy efforts by medical workers. The Peoria-area child, the now-teenaged James Fulton Engstrom, is slated to present relics of Sheen at the ceremony, accompanied by his family, who had sought Sheen's intercession for healing.</p><p>His mother, Bonnie Engstrom, said today's ceremony will feel like a “foretaste of heaven.”</p><p>She and her husband taught each of their eight children to have a devotion to their patron saint, giving them the sense that they have a heavenly “squad” cheering them on. They chose Sheen for James' patron after discovering the prelate's old videos, adding that his Midwestern-accented voice reminded her of her grandfather and great-grandfather. “He’s like a local boy,” she said at a morning news conference.</p><p>James, who just turned 16, has a devotion to Sheen, but he's largely avoiding the media spotlight. “He’s a delightful young man, but he’s still just a teenage boy, and he needs to be given the space and the grace to have his own journey of life," Engstrom said. "He didn’t ask for any of this.”</p><p>She said she'd been praying to Sheen throughout the pregnancy, and “it was just a very natural thing in the hardest hour of our life” to seek his prayers. James was born at home without a pulse and rushed to the hospital — where workers who were attempting to resuscitate him were about to declare him deceased — when his heart began beating normally, Engstrom and other witnesses said.</p><h3>Sheen’s beatification backstory</h3><p>The beatification was originally scheduled for 2019, but the Vatican delayed the ceremony. The Diocese of Rochester, which Sheen briefly led in the 1960s, requested the delay out of caution, due to legal investigations taking place then into the oversight of priests accused of sexual abuse across New York state.</p><p>Church officials later concluded that Sheen’s record gave no cause for further delay, and plans for the ceremony resumed. Pope Leo XIV approved the beatification earlier this year.</p><p>“May the example and the intercession of this holy bishop, known for his evangelizing work through the media, inspire many others likewise to find new ways of spreading the gospel message with joyful enthusiasm,” Leo said Wednesday on the eve of the ceremony.</p><p>Monsignor Jason Gray, executive director of the Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen Foundation, said church investigators review records and interview witnesses before determining whether a healing qualifies as a miracle. He said there are now six more cases under investigation; a second miracle would qualify Sheen for sainthood under Vatican rules.</p><p>Peoria Bishop Louis Tylka said he believes the wait for canonization will be shorter than for the beatification, especially with an Illinois-born pope who's “very much aware of who Sheen is and how he influenced his own life.”</p><p>___</p><p>Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s <a class="Link" href="https://bit.ly/ap-twir" target="_blank" >collaboration</a> with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content.</p>

entries.title: Story behind Connor Onion's rise from La Grange to Fox Sports is sweet
entries.summary: <p>His name is Connor Onion, but he won’t make you cry.</p><p>If you’ve heard him broadcast games for Fox Sports, you already know that. What you might not know is that he could’ve been Connor O’Onion — pronounced O’Own-yun.</p><p>“It was O’Onion when my family was in Ireland,” Onion told the Sun-Times. “They came to the United States and dropped the ‘O’ to try to assimilate and naturally became farmers.</p><p>“An agriculture family with the last name Onion, I was told it was good for business. And they were also growing onions.”</p><p>Decades later, Onion was courtside with the man who turned the vegetable into a catchword. In 2023, Onion called a game with renowned college basketball analyst Bill Raftery — “Onions!” — and gifted him onions from his family on the air.</p><p>The story is so sweet, it actually might make you cry.</p><p>But enough onion jokes. The point is, Onion, a La Grange native and Lyons graduate, has made a name for himself in broadcasting. This summer, after Jason Benetti left for NBC, Fox promoted Onion, 31, to its No. 2 college football crew alongside analyst Robert Griffin III and reporter Alexa Landestoy. They’ll call the Northwestern-Indiana game Friday (7 p.m., Fox 32, 720-AM).</p><p>But in high school, Onion was focused more on becoming an athlete than a broadcaster. When he visited Ball State, he hoped to walk on to the football team. Then-coach Pete Lembo sized up the 5-11 Onion — wearing six pairs of socks to look taller — and probably thought, “Are you serious?”</p><p>“I think Coach Lembo had seen that trick before,” Onion said. “He was nice about it, but he was like, ‘I’ve seen the few highlights you have from high school. I think it’s probably time you consider a different profession.’ So that put me on the path to start pursuing broadcasting.”</p><p>During his senior year, Onion applied for 50 jobs broadcasting minor-league baseball. Five teams responded, two granted him interviews and one gave him an offer for the 2017 season — the Quad Cities River Bandits, then the Astros’ Single-A affiliate.</p><p>That job put him on the air every day, giving him the repetition to improve. His job that fall, calling sports at Southern Illinois, gave him the chance to sharpen his skills, thanks in large part to Mike Reis, who retired in 2023 after 44 seasons calling SIU sports.</p><p>“We had a lot of conversations in his office in Carbondale where he told me, ‘Connor, I think you’ve got potential, but you’ve got a lot of getting better to do,’ ” Onion said. “I was crushed when he would sit me down and tell me that I wasn’t very good. I have a lot of where this thing has taken me because of the guidance that Mike Reis has given me.”</p><p>“You don’t ask for criticism if you think you’re really good,” Reis said. “It starts with ego and being a good person, believing you’re not the star. Those are character things that are in Connor’s favor that led to the success that he’s having at an early age.”</p><p>At SIU, Onion called women’s volleyball. That helped him get a job in 2021 at Big Ten Network, which was starting to air more volleyball. He added Big Ten basketball and football to his resume, and that helped him get a job in 2024 with Fox, which co-owns BTN with the conference.</p><p>Bulls fans should remember Onion from his time subbing for TV voice Adam Amin last year. The Bulls had three consecutive remarkable games out West, a double-overtime loss to the Jazz and thrilling wins over the Nuggets and Trail Blazers. Onion called them as if he had been doing the job for years. As a lifelong Bulls fan, it was a special experience.</p><p>“I was born right in the middle of the two three-peats,” he said. “The joke in my family is that my birth certificate says, ‘Time of birth: End of Bulls game,’ because everybody’s eyes were glued to the Bulls instead of delivering me into the world.”</p><p>Now all eyes are on him as he calls college football, college basketball, volleyball and baseball for Fox. In fact, after calling Northwestern-Indiana, he’ll drive to Indianapolis, get a few hours of sleep and fly out Saturday morning to call Orioles-Yankees at night. Next Friday, he, Griffin and Landestoy will call Penn State-Northwestern, the first game at the new Ryan Field.</p><p>They’re plum assignments for Onion, who has an excellent voice, command of his broadcasts and a minimalist style. He also has an endearing humility, as shown in another onion story.</p><p>When schools shut down during the pandemic, one of Onion’s odd jobs was selling onions at a farmer’s market in La Grange. The farmers he worked for, from Michigan, thought he was just a neighborhood kid who needed some extra cash. Eventually, his broadcasting came up.</p><p>“There’s some Michigan State fans that are part of that farm that have seen the games that I’ve done since then,” Onion said. “That’s been funny to revisit.”</p><p>Enough to make you cry.</p>

entries.title: Trabajadores de hoteles del centro de Chicago votan para autorizar una huelga
entries.summary: <p>Miles de trabajadores de hoteles de Chicago podrían ir a la huelga en cualquier momento.</p><p>Los miembros de Unite Here Local 1 votaron el lunes por la noche para autorizar una huelga; su contrato actual venció el 31 de agosto.</p><p>“El turismo en Chicago está en auge, mientras la inflación sigue aumentando, y eso está afectando a nuestros trabajadores hoteleros en toda la industria”, dijo en un comunicado del sindicato Karen Kent, presidenta de Unite Here Local 1.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-610000" name="module-610000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Sienten el peso cada vez que van al supermercado a comprar comida, o cuando regresan a casa del trabajo y están demasiado cansados para pasar tiempo con su familia. Los trabajadores están listos para irse a la huelga porque trabajan demasiado duro para vivir así”.</p><p>Local 1 representa a personal de limpieza, cocineros, lavaplatos, agentes de recepción, meseros y trabajadores de servicio de alimentos.</p><p>Más del 85% de los trabajadores votó a favor de ir a la huelga en la primera ronda de votación, según un comunicado del sindicato. El sindicato ha estado negociando desde junio con representantes de 46 hoteles. La mayoría pertenece a tres grandes grupos hoteleros —Hyatt, Marriott y Hilton— aunque también hay algunos operadores más pequeños.</p><p>La mayoría de los trabajadores —unos 7,000— están en el centro de la ciudad.</p><p>Basado en una encuesta entre sus miembros, el sindicato dijo que alrededor de un tercio no puede cubrir la renta o la hipoteca, mientras que dos tercios vieron reducidas sus horas durante el periodo de baja actividad. Mientras tanto, 1 de cada 4 trabajadores recurrió a préstamos de cheque o de corto plazo para cubrir gastos.</p><p>Según Local 1, los operadores hoteleros Marriott, Hyatt y Hilton devolvieron $22,300 millones a sus accionistas en los últimos tres años.</p><p>El martes, algunos miembros del sindicato estaban en la Universidad East-West, en el Loop, donde podían inscribirse para recibir los beneficios disponibles del sindicato si los trabajadores deciden ir a la huelga.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Cubs clinch postseason spot with win over Marlins, wild-card seeding still a mystery
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are, officially, going to be playing playoff baseball.</p><p>They clinched a spot in baseball’s postseason Thursday with a 2-1 win over the Marlins.</p><p>Right fielder Seiya Suzuki’s solo home run tied the game at 1 in the fifth inning, and an inning later, second baseman Nico Hoerner followed left fielder Ian Happ’s leadoff triple with a go-ahead RBI single.</p><p>But lefty starter Matthew Boyd was the hero of the day, throwing seven innings of one-run ball to not only keep the Marlins at bay but also preserve Craig Counsell’s bullpen ahead of Friday’s doubleheader in Boston.</p><p>The Cubs started the day likely to make it into the tournament, with a magic number of one, requiring just one win — or one Diamondbacks loss — in their final four games to make it happen.</p><p>At least on that front, there will be no more scoreboard-watching, with Thursday’s victory advancing them into the playoffs.</p><p>As for what seed they’ll be on the NL side of the bracket and where they’ll be playing their opening-round, best-of-three series, that all remains to be figured out.</p><p>They started Thursday tied with the Phillies for second place in the wild-card standings, both teams a single game behind the first-place Padres. The Cubs hold the tiebreakers with both teams, but they’re bunched-up enough that the final few regular-season games will determine who finishes where.</p><p>Earning the top wild-card spot and the No. 4 seed means the Cubs would host an opening-round series at Wrigley Field. Taking the second wild-card spot and the No. 5 seed would send the Cubs on the road against the top-finishing wild-card team. And landing in the No. 6 spot, as the third wild-card team, would mean a visit to the NL East-winning Braves in Atlanta.</p><p>The Cubs travel to finish their regular-season schedule with three games against the Red Sox this weekend in Boston. That series has already been jumbled by forecasted rainstorms, with Sunday’s originally scheduled season finale moved to Friday as part of the aforementioned doubleheader.</p><p>The wild-card round of the playoffs begins Tuesday.</p>

entries.title: Man who painted hate symbols at Northwestern University sentenced to 7 years in prison
entries.summary: <p>A man who defaced property at Northwestern University with hateful symbols was sentenced to seven years in prison.</p><p>Shahid Hussain, 43, of Niles, pleaded guilty on Thursday to two counts of hate and one count of institutional vandalism. Cook County Judge Paul Pavlus sentenced Hussain during a hearing in Skokie.</p><p>Hussain was accused of entering the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/06/northwestern-university-investigating-hate-symbols-found-on-campus" target="_blank" >Northwestern campus</a> on Jan. 30 to draw swastikas and other Nazi symbols on numerous signs and other university property. Surveillance video also shows him raising his arm in a Nazi salute.</p><p>“Acts of hate and intimidation have no place in our communities,” State’s Attorney Eileen Burke said in a statement. “This guilty plea and prison sentence demonstrate that we will hold individuals accountable for crimes intended to intimidate and spread hate in our communities.”</p><p>Evanston police found Hussain, and Northwestern police arrested him on Feb. 12, when he admitted to defacing the property with Nazi symbols, prosecutors said.</p><p>It wasn’t the first time.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/2/1/22912695/hate-crime-charges-man-accused-of-painting-swastikas-on-synagogue-jewish-high-school" target="_blank" >In 2022</a>, Hussain was convicted of hate crime and institutional vandalism for incidents involving a Jewish day school, several synagogues and a kosher bakery. He was sentenced to three years in the Illinois Department of Corrections.</p><p>Northwestern University did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: White Sox clinch first playoff berth since 2021 with 9-1 blowout win over Royals
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. – In a season with 11 walk-off victories, 35 come-from-behind wins, 31 usages of an opener, and countless defied expectations, the White Sox clinched their first playoff berth in five years on Thursday with a drama-free 9-1 blowout of the last-place Royals.</p><p>After a week full of pondering season-series tiebreakers and which stragglers in the American League Wild Card race needed to lose to enable the Sox to clinch, they entered Thursday afternoon with a much clearer mandate: win, and they would be in. Even with the division race against the Cleveland Guardians going down to the wire, guaranteeing postseason baseball of any stripe was plenty of incentive.</p><p>“I haven’t popped bottles or anything in a while and you never know when you’re going to have a chance to do it again,” outfielder Andrew Benintendi told the Sun-Times before driving in a pair of runs on Thursday. “Obviously we want to win the division. Hopefully we can pop twice in the next four days.”</p><p>And with that, the Sox offense jumped all over Royals starter Randy Dobnak for six runs in the first two innings of a game that never was in doubt. The mildly eyebrow-raising decision to start rookie David Sandlin without an opener produced six innings of one-run ball with a career-high seven strikeouts.</p><p>It was only this April that the Sox snapped a 14-game losing streak at Kauffman Stadium, yet the mistakes that historically marked their struggles in Kansas City were occurring on the other side.</p><p>After Sam Antonacci led off the game with a single, Dobnak’s throw on a Kyle Teel bunt attempt dragged first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino off the bag, helping to key a three-run first. The same story played out an inning later. Antonacci followed a Braden Montgomery leadoff single with a walk, and Dobnak compounded the problem with a quick pickoff move to first, only to find that Pasquantino wasn’t holding the runner nor expecting a throw. Montgomery scored all the way from second as the ball rattled around in foul territory, kickstarting another three-run frame. When longtime Sox villain Salvador Perez lined a solo home run in the fourth, it only made it a 8-1 game.</p><p>Each of the top-three hitters in the Sox lineup reached base at least three times. Antonacci scored thrice on the afternoon, Teel blasted his fifth homer of the year out to center in the fourth, and reigning AL Player of the Week Miguel Vargas both scored and drove in a pair of runs.</p><p>No team in MLB history has ever made the playoffs immediately after three consecutive years of 100 losses or more, until these 2026 White Sox pulled it off with three games to spare. That means there’s plenty of work to be done, as Thursday’s win pulls the Sox within a half-game of the Guardians in the AL Central standings. But there’s also plenty to celebrate.</p><p>“Obviously, we’ll continue to do our jobs,” said Davis Martin, the longest-tenured player on the team. “But it means the world today.”</p>

entries.title: 'Broadview Six' prosecutor breaks silence, says she 'owns' mistakes but there's 'no basis' for smears
entries.summary: <p>The prosecutor at the center of Chicago's "Broadview Six" scandal broke her silence Thursday, insisting through her attorneys that she followed the instructions of U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros' front office "at every turn" during her handling of the tainted case.</p><p>In a surprise 16-page court filing, her legal team also disclosed that "the U.S. Attorney directed Ms. Mecklenburg to order an expedited copy" of an Oct. 9 grand jury transcript that documented apparent misconduct by Mecklenburg. </p><p>Boutros has acknowledged receiving the transcript by email last fall, but he said he doesn't remember reading it. He told U.S. District Judge April Perry in May that he'd learned of problems in that grand jury session in late April.</p><p>Mecklenburg's attorneys also wrote Thursday they were told by Boutros' office that Mecklenburg "could be disciplined or terminated" for filing anything in court on her own behalf. Therefore, they wrote, Mecklenburg has retired from the Justice Department, effective Thursday.</p><p>"To the extent that Ms. Mecklenburg made mistakes … she owns them," attorneys Sergio Acosta and Joel Bertocchi wrote.</p><p>However, they said attorneys for the former defendants in the case had gone too far, and "there is no basis for them to smear her with meritless accusations that she lied or acted in bad faith." </p><p>Mecklenburg's attorneys filed Thursday's motion in a conditional bid to intervene in the "Broadview Six" case. They say they want to be heard if Perry grants a defense motion for a sanctions hearing or to appoint a special counsel. Perry has said she'll hear oral arguments on those motions Oct. 1.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” prosecution revolved around an Operation Midway Blitz protest on Sept. 26, 2025. Prosecutors alleged a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV outside an immigration facility in west suburban Broadview. But from that crowd, only six people were charged with conspiring<b> </b>to impede<b> </b>a federal agent.</p><p>Most of the six were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/01/broadview-six-midway-blitz-abughazaleh-straw-rabbit-perry-trump-ice-crime" target="_blank" >Those charged</a> were then-congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b> </b>campaign worker Andre Martin.</p><p>The one-year anniversary of their protest is Saturday.</p><p>The feds dropped charges against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Sharp</a><b> </b>in March. Then, on the eve of trial in late May, defense attorneys convinced Perry<b> </b>to review unredacted transcripts<b> </b>of grand jury proceedings<b> </b>in the case. The feds had previously given her redacted versions.</p><p>Perry later said she was “incredibly shocked”<b> </b>to find three types of prosecutorial misconduct in the unredacted transcripts. Mecklenburg<b> </b>is accused of speaking with grand jurors outside the grand jury room. She's also accused of excusing grand jurors who didn’t agree with the feds’ case — a claim Mecklenburg's attorneys deny.</p><p>She’s also accused of a forbidden practice known as “vouching.”<b> </b>It occurs when prosecutors put their personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges. Grand jurors are expected to hand up indictments based on evidence, not the goodwill of a prosecutor who already has the upper hand in the grand jury room.</p><p>Perry also mentioned a fourth concern: The alleged misconduct had been redacted out of the transcripts initially given to her by the feds. She called that “the most problematic”<b> </b>issue of all.</p><p>But Mecklenburg withdrew from the "Broadview Six" case in February. Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan has taken responsibility for the redactions, instead.</p><p>Boutros personally dropped<b> </b>the charges against the four defendants who nearly went to trial. He’s since acknowledged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/05/boutros-broadview-six-perry" target="_blank" >“mistakes were made.”</a><b> </b>But he said he’s implemented reforms to prevent them from happening again. He noted his office is not accused of explicitly violating any order from Perry regarding the grand jury transcripts.</p><p>Still, he<b> </b>admitted<b> </b>the<b> </b>“better course”<b> </b>would have been to give her unredacted copies of the grand jury transcripts in the first place.</p>

entries.title: CPS enrollment drops again amid low birth rates and immigrant fears
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools enrollment has declined once again by another 11,500 students to about 304,700, officials said Thursday in announcing preliminary data, the lowest number in more than two decades.</p><p>Enrollment had stabilized for two years — even increasing briefly — with the arrival of thousands of immigrant students in 2023 and 2024. But the trend proved short-lived as the district’s 20-year enrollment freefall resumed last year and again this fall, dwindling from its high of nearly 439,000 students in the 2002-2003 school year.</p><p>Declining enrollment — and, subsequently, underenrolled schools — have become a key issue in the city’s first-ever <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/09/24/school-board-election-2026-president-candidates-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u>school board president race</u></a> as some candidates suggest revisiting school closures. The district has a moratorium on closings until after this school year. Community groups rallied Thursday morning to call for the prohibition to be extended.</p><p>CPS officials are pointing to declining birth rates locally, nationally and globally, in addition to families leaving the city for the suburbs and immigrant population declines spurred by President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation policies.</p><p>“Here’s the bottom line: What we control is the quality of education and experience that we provide our students,” CPS Supt./CEO Macquline King told the Board of Education in its monthly meeting Thursday. “That’s what our families care about, and that has been my focus as superintendent/CEO — investing in students, improving the student experience and working with our school communities to help every student reach their potential.”</p><p>King said the silver lining is that, despite another decline, CPS has regained its status as the nation’s third-largest public school system.</p><p>“I know, it’s like winning because someone tripped, but we are the third largest district in the country again,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Longtime and widespread trends</h3><p>Leaders tried to contextualize the declines by showing that public school enrollment is falling nationwide, particularly in large urban districts. From 2014 to 2024, the most significant enrollment losses have happened in Los Angeles, Houson, Chicago, Dallas and Philadelphia, according to data presented by CPS officials.</p><p>Illinois has also lost about 200,000 public school students statewide, or 10%, since 2017.</p><p>Anniese Lewis, the deputy chief education officer at CPS, said districts still have not recovered from steep declines during the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>Lewis cited falling birthrates nationally that are “even more pronounced here in Chicago.”</p><p>In 2005, there were about 45,000 births in Chicago. That fell by more than 40% to around 27,000 in 2023. The district’s kindergarten cohort has shrunk by the thousands.</p><p>“Most recently, we’ve dipped below the national average,” Lewis told the board Thursday.</p><p>The district has 450,000 available seats in its schools with 455,000 school-age children in Chicago in 2024, the year with the most recent count. With the share of Chicago students enrolled in private school or classified in census data as “not enrolled” — which includes children who are homeschooled, have dropped out or are in between schools — slightly increasing, CPS has been left with more empty seats.</p><p>Between 2008 and 2018, CPS served roughly 75% of the city’s school-age population. By 2023, that had fallen to 71%,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/20/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-cps-birth-rates-private-school-kids-first" target="_blank" >according to a report</a> from the advocacy group Kids First Chicago.</p><p>The biggest declines over the past decade have been in some of Chicago’s immigrant community hubs, such as Pilsen , Little Village, Avondale, Brighton Park, Gage Park and McKinley Park — in some cases seeing as dramatic of decreases as 53% in the past decade, according to CPS.</p><p>“There has been a rapid gentrification leading to a steep decline in [the] youth population. Multigenerational family homes are being converted to single-family homes, reducing the availability of family housing,” Lewis said. “[And] there has been an exodus of working class families who are moving to the outer suburbs for single family homes and perceived safety.”</p><p>Those trends were apparently accelerated by the Trump administration’s damaging deportation campaign last fall. Some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/28/mather-senior-laces-up-his-soccer-shoes-again-after-months-in-immigration-detention" target="_blank" >students were detained,</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" >federal activity around schools</a> stoked fear in immigrant communities. There <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/12/cps-should-work-to-prevent-future-attendance-drops-due-to-immigration-enforcement-community-groups-say" target="_blank" >were spikes in absenteeism</a> among English language learners who chose to stay home during enforcement actions. Some families considered leaving the city to escape the threat.</p><p>“While the U.S. experienced an influx of new arrivals in 2023 and 2024, this trend has now reversed dramatically,” Lewis said. “We are all familiar with the changes in immigration policy and enforcement at the federal level. Fewer people are coming into the US and more are leaving.”</p><p>At Kelly College Prep in Brighton Park, enrollment this year fell by 229 students to 1,273, according to preliminary data.</p><p>Meanwhile in the past 10 years, CPS enrollment has increased, in some cases significantly, around more affluent areas such as O’Hare, the Loop, Lincoln Park, North Center, Near South Side and Kenwood.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d70000" name="image-d70000"></a> <picture American students remained roughly the same among the 304,687 students enrolled at CPS on the 20th day of the school year, when the district takes its annual count.</p><p>The share of students in <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/07/18/cps-special-education-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>special education grew again</u></a>, up to 18.4% of CPS. But the district counted slightly fewer students who are in poverty, experiencing homelessness or learning English — though officials said those numbers typically go up after the start of the school year as students’ needs are identified.</p><p>Charter and contract schools saw slightly steeper enrollment declines than district-run schools, in part because five former Acero charter schools and ChiArts transitioned to traditional CPS schools.</p><h3>School board president race</h3><p>Ever since the highly controversial and historic <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>closing of 50 schools</u></a> by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel in 2013, closures have been a third-rail policy that most leaders have avoided suggesting.</p><p>But those conversations have reignited in this year’s school board president race, with three of four candidates indicating or outright saying they would consider school closings.</p><p>One candidate, Victor P. Henderson, responded to a WBEZ, Sun-Times and Chalkbeat candidate questionnaire that he would be open to closing schools “as an extraordinary last resort.” Sendhil Revuluri said he also would be willing to close schools to improve the experiences of students in schools that have become too small to meet their academic and social needs.</p><p>Challenger and current board member Jessica Biggs declined to say yes or no, instead saying closings should be the “last thing” leaders propose but that “budget pressure is real.” Only Hilario Dominguez, backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, said he would oppose school closings.</p><p>Evidence has shown that the 2013 closings didn’t lead to lower costs, better outcomes for students or improved conditions in communities, the Sun-Times and WBEZ <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>found in an investigation a decade later.</u></a></p><p>Even so, enrollment is still tied to how CPS allocates its resources, despite the funding calculation having shifted to focus more on students’ needs in recent years. This year, the district planned to cut assistant principal positions at schools with fewer than 250 students to help stem its budget deficit.</p>

entries.title: Bears' first injury report has Caleb Williams, Tyson Bagent sitting out Thursday
entries.summary: <p>Neither Tyson Bagent nor Caleb Williams would have practiced Thursday if the Bears held one.</p><p>Case Keenum was the only healthy quarterback on the Bears' 53-man roster when they submitted their first injury report Thursday. The report was estimated, as the Bears didn't practice.</p><p>The Bears have other injury issues. Kicker Cairo Santos would not have practiced because of a right hip issue. Neither would running back Kyle Monangai, who has a knee injury. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson (hamstring) and defensive tackle Grady Jarrett (rest) would have sat out, too.</p><p>Santos being hampered would be a blow to an offense that managed three points last week. The Bears don't have a backup kicker and would have to add one during the week if they decide he's unlikely to play.</p><p>Bagent took over for Williams when the latter pulled his hamstring Sunday. He reported concussion symptoms Tuesday morning and was put into the league's five-step protocol. He did not go to Halas Hall on Wednesday. Players are allowed to practice while in the concussion protocol — the Vikings' Kyler Murray did three times last week but was not cleared to face the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>.</p><p>Williams won't practice all week, coach Ben Johnson said. He wouldn't rule Williams out for Monday's game, but it seems unlikely the Bears would rush him back.</p><p>Miller Moss, who spent training camp with the team and re-signed the day before its opener, is on the practice squad and will likely promoted to the active roster on Monday.</p><p>Defensive lineman Shemar Turner and linebacker Noah Sewell, who returned to practice off the physically-unable-to-perform list Wednesday, were limited. They can't play in games until Week 5.</p><p>The Bears also re-signed long snapper Beau Gardner to the practice squad two days after cut him. Receiver Scotty Miller, the Barrington High School alum and former Super Bowl champ, was cut to make room.<br></p>
