entries.title: Northwestern at Indiana? Illinois at Ohio State? Be afraid — very afraid? Week 4 college football picks
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Northwestern</a>’s and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Illinois</a>’ longest shots of the season are here.</p><p>Yay?</p><p><b>Northwestern (+21) at No. 5 Indiana </b>(7 p.m. Friday, Fox 32, 720-AM) looks a whole lot like a game the Wildcats can’t win. <b>Illinois (+27½) at No. 7 Ohio State </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32, 890-AM) seemingly shapes up likewise.</p><p>This is where money enters the conversation, because it has to.</p><p>A recent Athletic report put dollar estimates on the war chests for players at every Big Ten school. In ballpark terms, Ohio State ranked at the top of the conference in roster budget at around $50 million, with Indiana a couple of notches behind at closer to $40 million. Well down the list, in the low 20s — again, we’re talking millions — were the Wildcats and the Illini.</p><p>That’s still a heck of a lot of bread the lesser two programs are doling out, no doubt. But the discrepancies kind of put those three- and four-touchdown point spreads in perspective, don’t they?</p><p>“When [the NIL era started in 2021], I literally said, ‘Hey, if I’m within $2 million of Ohio State, Oregon, Penn State and Michigan, I’m good. Just let me go,” Illini coach Bret Bielema said this week. “When I’m within $25 million, I’m not so good.”</p><p>The economics of major college sports has become so extreme, it feels almost naive to size up some games in terms of X’s and O’s. But one supposes that’s why we’re all here, so — as I resist the urge to invoke the words “inevitable blowouts” — what’s going to happen on the field in these two contests?</p><p>Defending national champion Indiana has cake-walked through three games against North Texas, Howard and Western Kentucky by a combined score of 145-16. Transfer quarterback Josh Hoover has been flawless and transfer running back Turbo Richard explosive. Wideouts Charlie Becker and Nick Marsh — the latter a transfer, too — are as good a pair as the Wildcats will see. The Hoosiers’ defense is aggressive in a manner Bears fans might appreciate after seeing the relentless blitzing of the Vikings.</p><p>Sounds scary? It should.</p><p>The Wildcats (2-0) opened a lot of eyes last weekend in a 41-7 squashing of Colorado. They’re better than I thought they’d be. They might even have a little something for Penn State when the new Ryan Field opens next week. But back to reality: Hoosiers, 41-17.</p><p>As for the Illibuck Trophy game, have I mentioned the trophy is a wooden turtle? Would a trophy of a surfboard or a turkey club sandwich be any less apropos? But never mind that, back to the inevitable blow … oops, sorry.</p><p>The Buckeyes (2-1) haven’t quite reached ruthless-dream-killer mode yet, having lost by one point at Texas and not yet gotten their running game on track. But it’s coming. This is still a playoff team and still as towering a contender for the national championship as there is.</p><p>The Illini combo of QB Katin Houser and wideout Collin Dixon — who leads the nation with seven touchdown receptions — will make some noise. The first half might even be interesting. First quarter, at least?</p><p>If the Illini (2-1) have any pass rush to speak of, it better show up in a hurry. Otherwise, the deep shots from Julian Sayin to sensational receiver Jeremiah Smith will be like stealing candy from a baby turtle. Buckeyes, 38-14.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jeremiah Smith still went off in Ohio State’s heartbreaking loss to Texas<br><br>8 REC, 164 YDS, 1 TD <a href="https://t.co/bBYxw6eVwU">pic.twitter.com/bBYxw6eVwU</a></p>— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) <a href="https://x.com/NFLPerformances/status/2098973988395307058?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 13, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>OTHER WEEK 4 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday unless otherwise noted.</i></p><p><b>No. 4 Ole Miss (+3½) at No. 21 Florida </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): What goes up — the Rebels after an incredibly cathartic revenge win against Lane Kiffin — must come down. Gators by seven.</p><p><b>No. 17 Iowa (+5½) at No. 18 Michigan </b>(2:30 p.m., CBS 2): If you close your eyes and listen hard, you can hear the pads popping already. Wolverines, 20-13.</p><p><b>No. 23 Texas A&M (+8½) at No. 10 LSU </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): Not the mega-hyped event it promised to be before the Aggies lost to Kentucky and the Tigers lost to Ole Miss, but it won’t disappoint. Tigers, 37-34 (OT).</p><p><b>No. 20 Oregon (-3) at No. 12 USC </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5): If the Ducks lose two weeks after their embarrassing effort at Oklahoma State, they’ll assume the title of Most Disappointing Team of 2026 and all but kiss the playoff goodbye before the end of September. Wow! Nah. Ducks, 34-30.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 1 Texas (-4) at No. 14 Tennessee </b>(11 a.m., ABC 7): Have to roll with Longhorns QB Arch Manning in Uncle Peyton’s house. Why? As good as Vols QB Faizon Brandon has looked, he’s a freshman — and all it takes is one really bad freshman mistake.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Purdue (+28) vs. No. 3 Notre Dame </b>(1 p.m., Peacock, 780-AM): Of course the Boilermakers can’t win this game, but they can score — Irish by not enough.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>5-3 straight-up, 3-5 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>15-7 straight-up, 9-13 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/22/caleb-williams-injury-bears-eagles-mnf-chicago-philadelphia-vikings-soldier-field-nfl" >Bear With Me: Cooked without Caleb? Remember, Bears dominated Eagles last year despite Williams’ worst outing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/21/cubs-white-sox-chicago-pete-crow-armstrong-pca-alex-bregman-munetaka-murakami-will-venable-mlb" target="_blank" >Which Cubs and White Sox made it? Which didn’t? We present the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong clinches seventh 40-40 season in baseball history
entries.summary: <p>How’s this for an exclamation point on an MVP candidacy?</p><p>Pete Crow-Armstrong has a 40-40 season.</p><p>He stole his 40th base of the season in the first inning of Thursday afternoon’s game against the Marlins, clinching the seventh 40-homer, 40-steal campaign in baseball history, a feat that puts the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ superstar center fielder in one of the game’s most exclusive clubs.</p><p>“There are only so many guys in the game that can even think about accomplishing it,” team president Jed Hoyer said Tuesday. “It’s the best position-player season I’ve ever seen in my career. He’s going to win the MVP. He’s going to win the Hank Aaron Award. He’s going to win the Platinum Glove.</p><p>“It’s a special season.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong didn’t need to do this to win the NL MVP race he’s been in control of for the last couple months, but it’s likely to be the first line on his resume as he joins the distinctive half dozen to achieve the feat previously: Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024).</p><p>That’s the complete list, showing that even the recency of Acuna and Ohtani gaining membership in the 40-40 club doesn’t ding the rarity of the feat.</p><p>The Wrigley Field crowd certainly appreciated the magnitude of the moment, raining “M-V-P” chants down on Crow-Armstrong as he saluted them from second base.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">A tip of the cap from PCA to the fans at Wrigley Field 👏 <a href="https://t.co/uZDXI0VH1E">pic.twitter.com/uZDXI0VH1E</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2103192089307533669?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Everything Pete has done this year has been really incredible,” manager Craig Counsell said Wednesday. “That’s a milestone, but we’ve seen it all already this year. The [fans] here have celebrated him in a really cool way. I’ve never seen it before.</p><p>“He’s done so many great things, and he’s created so many special moments for everybody here this year.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has spent the entire season doing things that have rarely been accomplished in baseball history, his statistical output during a ridiculous month of June putting him in the same company as baseball immortals Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig.</p><p>His 42nd home run last week matched Hall of Famer and franchise legend Billy Williams for the most dingers in a single season by a left-handed hitting Cub, and he’s now in sole possession of that record, with 45.</p><p>“He moves differently. He has different tools than everyone else. And you just kind of enjoy sitting back and watching history being made,” designated hitter Michael Conforto said of his teammate last week. “He’s relentless in what he wants to achieve, definitely as a team, but also it’s clear he wants to be the best.</p><p>“It’s really cool to watch. It’s been really fun to be his teammate.”</p>

entries.title: Judge orders new inspection of South Deering funeral home where 56 bodies found
entries.summary: <p>A judge Thursday ordered another inspection of the South Chicago Chapel, where 56 decomposing bodies were found last month in the South Deering neighborhood. </p><p>The funeral home operators, Clark and Johanna Morgan, were also barred by court order from using, renting or leasing the funeral home at 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>Cook County Judge Federico Rodriguez made the decisions during a hearing at the Richard J. Daley Center after the city sued the Morgans over alleged building code violations at the now-shuttered South Deering business. </p><p>City attorneys said an inspection hasn't been performed since the initial one, shortly after the gruesome discovery. During the new inspection of the building, which the city wants to happen on Oct. 23 and will be a check of the interior of the building, the Morgans must be there in person, Rodriguez said. </p><p>Additionally during Thursday's hearing, the city’s Department of Buildings asked the judge to issue a fine of $11,500 per day for every day the violations are not corrected. The Morgans were not present at the hearing. But an attorney representing the couple said they did not object to the orders.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" >state shut down</a> South Chicago Chapel on Aug. 6 after receiving a tip that the Morgans were improperly storing bodies. Inside the funeral home, investigators found 56 bodies in various stages of decomposition.</p><p>Following the investigation, the IDFPR suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer’s license. The agency is now seeking to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/21/south-chicago-chapel-johanna-clark-morgan-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-revocation-hearing" target="_blank" >permanently revoke her license</a>.</p><p>Chicago police are also investigating what happened at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>Sitting in the courtroom hoping the Morgans would show up was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/30/south-chicago-chapel-decomposing-bodies-funeral-home-vigil-families" target="_blank" >Marketa Krisitofek</a>, a mother who has been searching for answers about what happened to her son’s remains since he died in a crash in November 2010.</p><p>Kristofek said the Morgans were responsible for her son’s remains when they operated Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights. Illinois State Comptroller Susana Mendoza <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" >shut down the crematory</a> last year for mishandling remains.</p><p>Kristofek filed more than 30 complaints about the Morgans with Mendoza’s office and the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. But she said little came of them.</p><p>Now, Kristofek said she wants to understand how state agencies allowed the couple to continue handling human remains despite the numerous complaints.</p><p>“They [the Morgans] were able to leave one site and come to another and operate despite having a revoked license,” said Kristofek.<br></p>

entries.title: Taylor McGregor leaving Cubs' Marquee Sports Network for ESPN
entries.summary: <p>Taylor McGregor, Marquee Sports Network's field reporter for Cubs broadcasts, is leaving the network to join ESPN full-time. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs’</a> regular-season home finale Thursday marks her last day. Marquee will look to replace her for next season. The rest of the network's crew will return. </p><p>McGregor will continue as a sideline reporter on ESPN's coverage of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" >college football.</a> She also has appeared on the network's college baseball and softball coverage. </p><p>McGregor, 33, has been with Marquee since it launched in February 2020. During that time, her national profile grew as her work at ESPN expanded into major college games. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/03/26/taylor-mcgregor-keli-mcgregor-marquee-sports-network-espn-chicago-cubs-colorado-rockies-alanna-rizzo-charissa-thompson-brian-griese-mike-mccarthy" >How Taylor McGregor turned public-speaking skills into broadcasting career</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"Anyone who has watched her work, both with us and increasingly on ESPN, can see that she is a rising star in the industry," said Colin Faulkner, Cubs chief commercial officer, who's overseeing Marquee's operations. "Taylor’s professionalism, preparation, and ability to connect with players, coaches, and fans have made her an outstanding member of our broadcast team.”<br> </p>

entries.title: Finance Committee backs $2.5 billion sale of Chicago parking meters after sweetening lopsided deal
entries.summary: <p>The City Council’s Finance Committee on Thursday approved New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners’ $2.53 billion <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/chicago-parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-city-council-compromise-explainer" >bid to acquire Chicago parking meters, </a>along with a compromise aimed at making the widely despised meter deal less onerous for taxpayers.</p><p>“We were handed a lemon and we made lemonade,” Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd), one of a handful of City Council leaders who helped broker the deal, told fellow committee members. </p><p>Calling former Mayor Richard M. Daley’s 2008 decision to lease Chicago parking meters to private investors for 75 years “an example of what not to do,” Dowell said Chicagoans from “every corner of the city have become increasingly disillusioned” with a deal that allowed private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi to recoup their $1.15 billion investment two-fold with 57 years to go on the deal.</p><p>The committee passed the measure, with only two Council members, Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) and Ald. William Hall (6th) voting against it. The full City Council must still approve the proposed deal.</p><p>“Today is a historic day," Dowell said. "Today, we have the opportunity to not only apologize” to taxpayers who got the short end of the deal, “but back it up with real tangible benefits for the first time.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-190000" name="image-190000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3871229/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4030080/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77aa49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd)." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77aa49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f373cde/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77aa49c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4338x2435+0+229/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4b%2Fe6432e445672227890282b465fc0%2Fcouncil-112719-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd). </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), an investment banker, rained on Dowell’s parade. He argued that after Stonepeak deducts interest expenses and adds the potential for depreciation, the estimated benefit for Chicago taxpayers has been “wildly overstated by more than $100 million.”</p><p>“It’s still a win, but not as big a win as I thought it was,” Conway said.</p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) applauded his colleagues for doing what they could to level the playing field, but he said, “It’ll take a lot of sugar to get this [sour] deal sweet.”</p><p>Beale also demanded a guarantee that Stonepeak's promise to pay the city $75 million up-front and 5% profit-sharing — or $376.2 million over the course of the agreement — be earmarked to chip away at Chicago’s $36 billion mountain of unfunded pension liabilities. The deal also would reduce costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p></p><p>The City Council is facing a Sept. 30 deadline to either approve Stonepeak Partners’ $2.5 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters, or roll the dice in arbitration and in court.</p><p>Before casting that controversial vote, City Council leaders brokered a compromise after Mayor Brandon Johnson submitted four bids to take back the meters for as much as $3.2 billion — only to later abandon those efforts. </p><p>With no direction from the mayor, Dowell said she and a handful of other veteran alderpersons “took the bull by the horns and did the work" to make the deal better. Stonepeak also agreed to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. </p><p>And it agreed to explore creating entire non-metered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.”</p><p>Dowell told her colleagues that the “divestiture certificate” from Stonepeak pledging to unload Omni International was available for them to see. <br>The promise to sell Omni International was not enough to satisfy Ervin, who played the role of naysayer throughout Thursday’s hearing after pushing an 11th-hour plan to create a public infrastructure trust to take back the parking meters.</p><p>He demanded to know the value of Omni and wondered whether Stonepeak was “willing to walk away at a loss to do this” and what would happen if the selling price turns out to be too low. “What do we do then?” asked Ervin. </p><p>Losing patience, Dowell said, “You’ve made your point. You don’t like this deal. Let’s move on.”</p><p>Ervin also questioned why the city didn’t hold out for a share of Stonepeak’s gross revenues instead of settling for net revenues. When retiring Corporation Counsel Mary Richardson-Lowry noted that the compromise she helped to negotiate delivered “dollars the city never had before,” Ervin said, “And may never get.”</p><p>Ald. Nick Sposato (38th) offered a counterpoint to Ervin’s remarks. “This is a major coup for us… I am jumping for joy and giddy about this. I’m glad I’m part of a major accomplishment on our watch as opposed to what happened almost twenty years ago,” Sposato said.</p><p></p><p>In 2008, Daley leased the city’s 36,000 parking meters for 75 years to a private investment consortium for $1.15 billion. He used those proceeds to avoid raising property taxes at a time when city employee pension funds were sinking deeper in the hole. The lopsided deal sold off an asset that was generating revenue for the city. Motorists paid the price with steep rate hikes. </p><p>The Chicago Parking Meters LLC consortium formed by Morgan Stanley, Allianz and Sovereign Wealth recouped their initial $1.15 billion investment by 2019 — roughly 11 years into the 75-year lease.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>The deal also required the city to compensate Chicago Parking Meters LLC for every parking space taken out of service, either for a special event or construction project. That part of the deal alone has tied the city’s hands and cost Chicago taxpayers tens of millions of dollars.</p><p>The compromise isn't perfect. Ald. William Hall (6th) complained Thursday that African-American contractors were getting the short end of the stick. Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th) said there is "nothing there" in the divestiture certificate other than an email "stating an intent to sell" adding, "What happens if they don't?"</p><p>But the compromise does make the 2008 parking meter deal a bit less onerous.</p><p>“Every year, this asset has made a great deal of money for the purchasing party. We anticipate a little bit of that coming our way,” Richardson-Lowry said.</p><p></p><p>The sale to Stonepeak and the compromise attached to it still must be approved by the full City Council — either at a meeting scheduled for Friday, or on Tuesday if the transaction is deferred and published. If the Council rejects the deal or fails to meet the revised Sept. 30 deadline, the risk to Chicago taxpayers is great. It could cost the city millions.</p><p>The Morgan Stanley-led investment group could first ask an independent arbitrator to order the City Council to approve the sale or pay an exorbitant penalty, then file a lawsuit.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p> <p></p><p></p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Syrian refugee with genetic disorder in suburban Chicago faces looming cutoff from Medicaid
entries.summary: <p>Omar spent a recent morning like most teenagers — browsing YouTube videos ranging on topics from tech to anime.</p><p>But Omar wasn’t swiping through the videos with his fingers. The 19-year-old, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, uses his eyes to control the tablet, and he spends his days on a hospital bed that sits in the family’s small suburban living room. A window next to his bed looks out to their apartment complex. An entertainment center — decorated with Dragon Ball Z figurines — serves as storage for medical supplies to help care for the teen.</p><p>His parents, Mahmoud and Asmaa, are his caretakers with his mother often sleeping next to him on the family’s beige and red couch. The Sun-Times is not using the family’s last name due to their pending application for permanent residency. Omar’s parents say they worry what will happen to his health come Oct. 1 when they, along with an estimated 9,300 other immigrants in Illinois, are expected to lose Medicaid coverage.</p><p>“They’re caught between two fronts, really,” said Al Peters, director of immigration services at the Syrian Community Network. “They’ve lost their benefits, and they are not getting their next step in the process — their green card.”</p><p>As part of H.R.1, more commonly known as One Big Beautiful Bill, refugees will no longer be eligible to receive Medicaid, a state-federal program that provides health coverage to low-income households and people living with disabilities. It’s part of a larger overhaul the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/09/11/illinois-alerts-more-than-700-000-they-will-or-could-lose-medicaid-public-health-insurance" target="_blank" ><u>Trump administration is making to Medicaid</u></a> including new work requirements.</p><p>The last day of Medicaid coverage for this population will be Sept. 30. The Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services described the changes to Medicaid as a “cruel measure,” and said it’s the start of a larger effort to leave hundreds of thousands of people in the state without access to care.</p><p>“We are deeply concerned about the impact to families, especially as non-citizens have fewer options to gain medical coverage. This is the result of the federal law, and unfortunately, there is no recourse for impacted non-citizens to receive Medicaid unless the law is changed,” the department said in a statement.</p><div The family is concerned how the medicaid changes will affect the medical care their son receives.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Mark Black/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Refugees with permanent residency, or a green card, will remain eligible for the program, according to the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services.</p><p>But Omar’s family, who fled Syria, have been left in limbo as the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has slowed the processing of green card applications. Refugees were also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/09/snap-food-benefits-refugee-families-supplemental-food-assistance-program-asylum" target="_blank" ><u>cut off earlier this year from another safety-net program</u></a>, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.</p><p>Refugees are eligible to apply for permanent residency after one year in the country. At the Syrian Community Network, more than 780 refugees from various countries are waiting for their applications to be processed, Peters said.</p><p>The Syrian Community Network is pushing for USCIS to expedite Omar’s green card application, Peters said.</p><p>“The process as such is designed to frustrate and disappoint,” Peters said. “But in [Omar’s] case, that has potential fatal ramifications.”</p><h2>Stabilizing Omar’s health </h2><p>On top of a wooden cabinet, one machine monitors Omar’s oxygen while another one keeps tabs on his heart, Mahmoud said. Another machine is used to help feed him every day.</p><p>Mahmoud and his wife learned the intricacies of these machines that keep their son alive after arriving in the Chicago area in November 2023. Along a wall in the family’s living room, Mahmoud points to a chair they have learned to use to bathe Omar. A wheelchair tucked into a corner for the rare times they leave their apartment for doctor’s appointments.</p><p>“The situation for Omar now is stable,” Mahmoud said in Arabic through a translator.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bf0000" name="image-bf0000"></a> <picture were allowed to enter the United States through refugee resettlement, they said.</p><p>Omar was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy as a child, his parents said. People who have this type of genetic neuromuscular disorder are missing dystrophin, which helps keep muscle cells together and its absence leads to injury and loss of muscle function, according to the Muscular Dystrophy Association.</p><p>By 2016, the family had relocated to Egypt when Omar lost the ability to walk on his own, Mahmoud and Asmaa said. He was still able to eat on his own, but the family struggled to keep up with the physical therapy he needed and prioritized buying the medicines he needed, they said.</p><p>Then in January 2023 — just before they were scheduled to travel to the United States — Omar was hospitalized, Mahmoud and Asmaa said. He was no longer able to eat and breathe on his own and remained hospitalized for about a month and a half, they said.</p><p>Eventually they were able to travel to Chicago, and Omar spent his first months in the U.S. in late 2023 in various hospitals before his parents underwent a program that helped them learn how to become his caretakers, allowing Omar to live at home, his parents very dangerous,” Mahmoud said in Arabic through a translator, adding that every machine needs to work properly in order to keep him alive.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2025/06/21/medicaid-toddler-heart-transplant-kassandra-santos-marely-chavarria-santos-lurie-childrens-hospital" target="_blank" ><u>Medicaid covers all of the equipment</u></a> in the family’s living room that has become Omar’s makeshift care center, they said. The program also pays each month for their work as caretakers, Mahmoud said.</p><p>Asmaa, who tends to her son every time a machine beeps, would rather keep him at home, recalling how red his face turned anytime they left him in a hospital alone for a few hours.</p><p>“He’s not going to be comfortable at the hospital because he doesn’t speak very good English,” Asmaa said through a translator. “He’s going to be so anxious not understanding the language.”</p><h2>‘Living for our kid’</h2><p>Refugees had been eligible for Medicaid since at least 1996 though it’s likely they were eligible even before then, said Andrea Kovach, senior attorney with the Legal Council for Health Justice in Chicago.</p><p>The new eligibility changes will also result in a loss of coverage for immigrants seeking asylum and those who entered the country through humanitarian parole, such as those fleeing the war in Ukraine, according to the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services. Other immigrants like naturalized citizens, permanent residents, children and pregnant individuals will remain eligible.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, whose district includes the suburb where Omar’s family lives, couldn’t comment on specific cases her office is helping, but said many families are being devastated by federal changes.</p><p>“While my office is here to support my constituents in navigating their federal cases, it is clear we need bold legislation to address families' fear of losing their insurance. class="Figure-credit"><p>Mark Black/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Uninsured immigrants can still turn to community health centers, but advocates worry the change will increase avoidable hospital emergency room visits, Kovach said. That’s because refugees will remain eligible for emergency Medicaid, which is a way for a hospital to get reimbursed for treating an uninsured person facing a life-threatening health emergency.</p><p>“It has to be a serious medical emergency,” Kovach said. “That’s obviously not the most efficient way to get your healthcare. It’s not where individuals should go to get preventive care and screening.”</p><p>Refugees can purchase health insurance through the Affordable Care Act, known in the state as Get Covered Illinois, Kovach said. But starting in January, refugees will no longer be eligible for tax credits that make buying insurance through the marketplace more affordable, she said.</p><p>“Even though all of the qualified immigrant groups are technically eligible for ACA coverage after Jan. 1, they will no longer be eligible for the tax credits,” Kovach said. “That eligibility is really meaningless. It’s hollow.”</p><p>In mid-September, Mahmoud received a letter from Get Covered Illinois encouraging them to buy insurance through the marketplace.</p><p>“You are receiving this notice because the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services has determined that one or more members of your household do not qualify for Medicaid or All Kids,” the letter stated.</p><p>But as Mahmoud lists the family’s expenses — rent, utilities and phone bills — he’s not sure how they could afford to make ends meet without Medicaid. Mahmoud said he can get by without health insurance, but he says his son needs to stay on Medicaid.</p><p>“We are here, living for our kid,” Mahmoud said in Arabic through a translator.</p>

entries.title: Story behind Connor Onion's rise from La Grange to Fox Sports is sweet
entries.summary: <p>His name is Connor Onion, but he won’t make you cry.</p><p>If you’ve heard him broadcast games for Fox Sports, you already know that. What you might not know is that he could’ve been Connor O’Onion — pronounced O’Own-yun.</p><p>“It was O’Onion when my family was in Ireland,” Onion told the Sun-Times. “They came to the United States and dropped the ‘O’ to try to assimilate and naturally became farmers.</p><p>“An agriculture family with the last name Onion, I was told it was good for business. And they were also growing onions.”</p><p>Decades later, Onion was courtside with the man who turned the vegetable into a catchword. In 2023, Onion called a game with renowned college basketball analyst Bill Raftery — “Onions!” — and gifted him onions from his family on the air.</p><p>The story is so sweet, it actually might make you cry.</p><p>But enough onion jokes. The point is, Onion, a La Grange native and Lyons graduate, has made a name for himself in broadcasting. This summer, after Jason Benetti left for NBC, Fox promoted Onion, 31, to its No. 2 college football crew alongside analyst Robert Griffin III and reporter Alexa Landestoy. They’ll call the Northwestern-Indiana game Friday (7 p.m., Fox 32, 720-AM).</p><p>But in high school, Onion was focused more on becoming an athlete than a broadcaster. When he visited Ball State, he hoped to walk on to the football team. Then-coach Pete Lembo sized up the 5-11 Onion — wearing six pairs of socks to look taller — and probably thought, “Are you serious?”</p><p>“I think Coach Lembo had seen that trick before,” Onion said. “He was nice about it, but he was like, ‘I’ve seen the few highlights you have from high school. I think it’s probably time you consider a different profession.’ So that put me on the path to start pursuing broadcasting.”</p><p>During his senior year, Onion applied for 50 jobs broadcasting minor-league baseball. Five teams responded, two granted him interviews and one gave him an offer for the 2017 season — the Quad Cities River Bandits, then the Astros’ Single-A affiliate.</p><p>That job put him on the air every day, giving him the repetition to improve. His job that fall, calling sports at Southern Illinois, gave him the chance to sharpen his skills, thanks in large part to Mike Reis, who retired in 2023 after 44 seasons calling SIU sports.</p><p>“We had a lot of conversations in his office in Carbondale where he told me, ‘Connor, I think you’ve got potential, but you’ve got a lot of getting better to do,’ ” Onion said. “I was crushed when he would sit me down and tell me that I wasn’t very good. I have a lot of where this thing has taken me because of the guidance that Mike Reis has given me.”</p><p>“You don’t ask for criticism if you think you’re really good,” Reis said. “It starts with ego and being a good person, believing you’re not the star. Those are character things that are in Connor’s favor that led to the success that he’s having at an early age.”</p><p>At SIU, Onion called women’s volleyball. That helped him get a job in 2021 at Big Ten Network, which was starting to air more volleyball. He added Big Ten basketball and football to his resume, and that helped him get a job in 2024 with Fox, which co-owns BTN with the conference.</p><p>Bulls fans should remember Onion from his time subbing for TV voice Adam Amin last year. The Bulls had three consecutive remarkable games out West, a double-overtime loss to the Jazz and thrilling wins over the Nuggets and Trail Blazers. Onion called them as if he had been doing the job for years. As a lifelong Bulls fan, it was a special experience.</p><p>“I was born right in the middle of the two three-peats,” he said. “The joke in my family is that my birth certificate says, ‘Time of birth: End of Bulls game,’ because everybody’s eyes were glued to the Bulls instead of delivering me into the world.”</p><p>Now all eyes are on him as he calls college football, college basketball, volleyball and baseball for Fox. In fact, after calling Northwestern-Indiana, he’ll drive to Indianapolis, get a few hours of sleep and fly out Saturday morning to call Orioles-Yankees at night. Next Friday, he, Griffin and Landestoy will call Penn State-Northwestern, the first game at the new Ryan Field.</p><p>They’re plum assignments for Onion, who has an excellent voice, command of his broadcasts and a minimalist style. He also has an endearing humility, as shown in another onion story.</p><p>When schools shut down during the pandemic, one of Onion’s odd jobs was selling onions at a farmer’s market in La Grange. The farmers he worked for, from Michigan, thought he was just a neighborhood kid who needed some extra cash. Eventually, his broadcasting came up.</p><p>“There’s some Michigan State fans that are part of that farm that have seen the games that I’ve done since then,” Onion said. “That’s been funny to revisit.”</p><p>Enough to make you cry.</p>
